message.content:
/home/user/adss-2026-09-07 is an analytical data storage system in three layers, built in thin vertical slices,
each answering one business question end to end. DAS records what a source sent; DAB is the
business model (dab/model.yaml is THE ONLY PLACE THE DATA IS EXPLAINED, no source word in it);
DAR is a GENERATED Unified Star Schema -- one event bridge with a row per measurement event,
one peripheral per entity, one calendar. Keys inherit along many-to-one edges; measures do not.
destinations/app.py is a marimo page reading dar__uss only.

Slices 1-3 are done: orders placed per month and destination country; freight per customer
country and quarter (first relationship, first inherited key); orders shipped per month and days
to ship (second event on one entity, first derived value).

READ FIRST, they are the standard: /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/blueprint.md, /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/conventions.md,
/home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/deviations.md, ALL of /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/adr/*.md (0000-0008), /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/dab/model.yaml,
/home/user/adss-2026-09-07/dab/uss.yaml, /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/dab/mappings/*.yaml, /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/src/adss/uss.py,
/home/user/adss-2026-09-07/src/adss/mapping.py, /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/dar/uss/_bridge.sql, /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/das/contracts/*.yaml, and the
three directories under /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/questions/.

SLICE 4's question: "What revenue did we take per order month?" -- asked by a finance analyst.

It is the slice the whole architecture has been deferring to. THREE things land at once:

1. THE FAN-OUT PROOF. D-0001 (docs/deviations.md) departs from a DAR principle by putting every
   process in ONE shared dar__uss. Its whole justification is that a measure cannot multiply
   across a many-to-one walk. Slices 1-3 could not test it -- every entity was at one grain.
   Order lines are FINER than orders, so freight (on the order) and revenue (on the line) are
   the first two measures at different grains in one bridge. docs/deviations.md says in as many
   words that slice 4 is where the argument stops being carried on assertion.

2. A COMPOSITE SOURCE KEY. The source's OrderDetails entity has key (OrderId, ProductId) --
   both Edm.Int32. Conventions M2 permits exactly ONE primary_keys entry and says its VARCHAR
   result may be "a concat of casts with a separator", warning that a concat without a
   separator makes 'A1'+'23' and 'A12'+'3' the same key. That clause has been REVIEW-ONLY
   since slice 1 because nothing had a composite key. With integer ids the collision is live:
   order 121 product 3 versus order 12 product 13.

3. A FLOAT IN THE SOURCE. OrderDetail.Discount is Edm.Single -- a float. Revenue is
   quantity x unit price x (1 - discount). Slice 3 established (ADR 0007, and a data check in
   src/adss/checks.py) that a question's two answers are compared row by row BY VALUE, and that
   a float makes that comparison order-dependent because DuckDB's sum over doubles is not
   associative. Read that check and that ADR before deciding anything here.

HARD RULES FOR YOU
- Do NOT write, edit or create any file in /home/user/adss-2026-09-07; no git commands that change state. Work in
  /tmp. Reading and read-only commands are fine (uv run pytest, uv run adss check, read-only
  DuckDB against /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/warehouse.duckdb).
- Ground everything in what you actually read or ran. Quote file and line.

YOUR JOB: draft the options and consequences for the decisions this slice forces, so a MADR can
be written from each. You are not writing the records; you are doing the work they rest on.

DECISION A -- how a composite source key becomes one entity key.
M2 permits a concat of casts with a separator. Work out, concretely:
  - the exact expression, and what separator. Is a separator that can appear IN a value safe?
    Both parts are integers here, so is that reasoning "fine today, wrong at the first string
    key" -- and does that matter, given the key is loaded once and cannot be changed after?
  - M2 says two primary_keys entries are read as two ALTERNATE IDENTIFIERS and "cannot be undone
    once loaded". Verify that claim if you can, or say it is unverified.
  - What does the entity's key look like in dar__uss, and does anything downstream have to
    parse it back apart? If a question ever needs "which product", is the key the wrong place
    to get it from, and what is the right place?
  - Is there an option OTHER than concat? Consider: a surrogate, the source's own row identity,
    or refusing composite keys entirely and modelling the line differently. Say which you would
    argue for.

DECISION B -- how the fan-out proof is actually made.
This is the one that matters. D-0001 rests on "a measure is non-null only on the stage of the
(entity, event) that owns it, and every other branch emits a typed NULL". Work out:
  - the exact query a reader would write that COULD multiply freight across lines, and what the
    bridge returns for it instead. Construct both in a scratch DuckDB from the real warehouse
    if you can.
  - What TEST makes the property fail if the generator broke it? ADR 0002's Confirmation has
    been promising this test since slice 1. Where does it live -- tests/ (machinery, no
    business words, no warehouse) or checks/ (data, against the real build)? Draft it.
  - Is the property actually TRUE of the design, or only of the data? Say plainly if there is a
    shape in which it fails, and what that shape is.
  - What would a reader have to do WRONG to multiply the measure anyway, and does anything stop
    them? A bridge does not stop a bad query; it makes the good query natural. Is that enough
    for D-0001 to be closed, or does the deviation stay open with a narrower argument?

DECISION C -- the float discount.
  - What type should DAS give it? What does the engine do with a NUMBER attribute (the dab
    skill says DECIMAL(28,8), verify)? Where does the float stop being a float?
  - Revenue = quantity x price x (1 - discount). If discount is a float anywhere in that chain,
    is the product exact? Test it: compute revenue both ways over the real order lines, once
    with the discount as DOUBLE and once as DECIMAL, and see whether the totals differ and
    whether summing in different orders differs.
  - Does the exactness data check added in slice 3 catch it, and at which layer would it fire?
  - Is there a rounding decision to make -- and if so, whose is it, the model's or the
    question's? Money to how many places, and what does the model have to say for a check to be
    able to verify it?

For EACH decision: the options, what each costs in slices 5 and 6, which blueprint principle or
convention it satisfies and which it strains (QUOTE them), and the failure mode a reader six
months later hits. Draft the actual YAML and SQL.

Finally: name any decision this slice forces that I have NOT listed. Look hard at what a third
entity at a finer grain does to the bridge's published column contract, to the calendar, and to
entity_ids/entity_keys in src/adss/uss.py.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adss: The whole system — how the three layers fit, how a slice is built and accepted, and what to read before changing anything. Use when starting work on this repository, adding a slice or a business question, deciding which layer a change belongs in, or when a change seems to need two layers at once.
- dab: Work on the DAB layer — dab/model.yaml, the mappings, and the modelling engine. Use when adding an entity, attribute or relationship, editing anything under dab/, running install/deploy/execute, or debugging engine errors, history that looks wrong, or rows that multiply.
- dar: Work on the DAR layer — the generated Unified Star Schema, dab/uss.yaml, and the SQL under dar/uss. Use when adding an event or a measure, changing the bridge's column contract, debugging a total that is wrong or multiplied, or when generated SQL and the model have drifted.
- das: Work on the DAS layer — data contracts, the dlt landing zone, and the raw and staged views. Use when adding or changing a source, editing das/contracts/*.yaml, touching src/adss/{contract,das,landing,source}.py, re-recording fixtures, or debugging why a column is missing, mistyped, or duplicated in das__staged.
- destination: Work on the marimo destination — the page that presents a question and its answer, and the screenshots a slice is accepted on. Use when adding a page for a new question, changing a chart, or when a screenshot is blank, truncated or fails to render.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers a dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- grill-to-build: Interview to exhaustion, then a plan I confirm, then a  workflow per slice. Use for any build run from a brief.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

1	# Architectural blueprint
2	
3	This is the overarching document. It states what the system must achieve and the absolute
4	principles that support it. It names no technology, no tool, no modelling technique and no
5	process — those live in [conventions.md](conventions.md) and in [adr/](adr/README.md), and each
6	must justify itself against what is written here.
7	
8	That separation is the point. Every tool this system currently uses must be replaceable without
9	invalidating a single line below.
10	
11	## The vision
12	
13	An analytical data storage system is built for requirements that do not exist yet, and it is
14	changed from the inside by its own use: every question it answers expands what its users want to
15	ask next. It is therefore judged over a life cycle measured in decades, not over the delivery of
16	any one data product.
17	
18	Four qualities, in no priority order, because a design that sacrifices one for another is a
19	design that has failed:
20	
21	| Quality | What it means here |
22	|---|---|
23	| **Maintainable** | A change costs about the same in year ten as in year one. |
24	| **Scalable** | Adding a source or a consumer strengthens the system rather than making the next addition harder. |
25	| **Adaptable** | A source replacement, a new entity or a new relationship is absorbed without rewriting what already works. |
26	| **Good time to market** | Not the fastest possible way. Always within acceptable timing. |
27	
28	Speed is deliberately last-named and deliberately qualified. A system that answers today's
29	question fastest and next year's question not at all has optimised the wrong variable.
30	
31	## The three layers
32	
33	The layers are named for their **purpose**, never for their position or their quality grade.
34	They are not bronze, silver and gold; they are not staging, core and marts. Ask three people what
35	belongs in silver and you get four answers — and these names are also the principles, so a name
36	that does not carry a principle is a name that cannot be enforced.
37	
38	| Layer | Data according to… | What it is |
39	|---|---|---|
40	| **DAS** | the **System** | what the source sent us, as it sent it |
41	| **DAB** | the **Business** | what the business means by it, integrated and source-agnostic |
42	| **DAR** | the **Requirements** | what a particular consumer needs, shaped for them |
43	
44	## Flow
45	
46	Flow is one-directional and has exactly three rules. They are absolutes.
47	
48	| # | Rule | Why it matters |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| F1 | **Analytical usage reads only DAR.** | Consumption against DAS or DAB creates dependencies on structures whose whole purpose is to be free to change. The dependency is invisible until something breaks. |
51	| F2 | **DAR reads only DAB.** | A data product that reaches past the business layer to a source has bypassed the integration that makes numbers agree, and reintroduces the cascade the architecture exists to break. |
52	| F3 | **DAB reads only DAS.** | A source connection wired into the business layer means the source dependency was moved, not broken. |
53	
54	Each movement between layers does exactly **one** job: ingest, integrate, specialise. Code that
55	ingests and integrates, or integrates and shapes for a report, has collapsed two layers into one
56	and is not permitted regardless of how convenient it is.
57	
58	## Per-layer principles
59	
60	### DAS — data according to the system
61	
62	| # | Principle | Why it matters |
63	|---|---|---|
64	| S1 | **Capture and persist only.** No business logic, no interpretation, no enrichment. | Interpretation here buries a decision in the one layer that is supposed to make none, and disguises the next source change as a business change. |
65	| S2 | **Non-volatile.** Nothing is updated. Nothing is deleted. Every load is retained. | DAB and DAR must be rebuildable from DAS at any time without going back to the source. That is what makes changing the layers above it safe. |
66	| S3 | **Forgiving ingestion, strict unpacking.** Accept whatever arrives; enforce structure at the boundary out. | Committing to a schema at ingest turns every upstream change into lost data. Enforcing nothing on the way out turns every upstream change into a silent one. |
67	| S4 | **Every data point records where it came from and when.** | Without per-row provenance, an answer that looks wrong cannot be traced, and the only remaining move is to distrust the whole system. |
68	| S5 | **The source keeps its own words.** | A field renamed to a business term is an interpretation, and S1 forbids interpretations here. |
69	
70	### DAB — data according to the business
71	
72	| # | Principle | Why it matters |
73	|---|---|---|
74	| B1 | **Subject oriented.** Organised around business concepts, never around source systems. | The concepts outlive the systems that happen to record them. |
75	| B2 | **Integrated.** Semantically and structurally source-agnostic. | Adding a second source for a concept must not add a parallel structure, and removing one must not change any structure at all. This is the property that breaks the dependency. |
76	| B3 | **Time-variant.** Historized: every version retained, none overwritten. | An answer served last quarter must still be reproducible this quarter, or the system cannot be audited. |
77	| B4 | **Non-volatile.** Never updated, never deleted. | Same reason as B3, stated as a physical constraint rather than an intention. |
78	| B5 | **Atomic.** The atomic data point is the base of every semantic meaning. No aggregation, no bucketing, no pre-rollup. | An aggregate here is a requirement leaking down a layer, and it is the reason teams start demanding raw data. |
79	| B6 | **Reusable.** Nothing exists here because one consumer wanted it. | A construct that only makes sense given one requirement belongs in DAR. |
80	| B7 | **Change is additive.** A new attribute, entity or relationship is a new structure, never a modification of an existing one. | A modification has a regression surface. An addition does not. Repeated over the thousands of changes a platform absorbs, that difference is the whole ball game. |
81	| B8 | **Meaning is defined exactly once, here.** | Definitions that exist in two places drift, and the drift surfaces as two reports that disagree. |
82	
83	### DAR — data according to the requirements
84	
85	| # | Principle | Why it matters |
86	|---|---|---|
87	| R1 | **Requirement oriented.** Shaped for a specific consumer, optimised for them. | The integration work is already done; this layer's only job is to be usable. |
88	| R2 | **No cross-dependency.** A data product owns its structures and does not consume another product's. Duplication between products is accepted deliberately. | Each product has its own rate of change. Sharing structure couples those rates and reintroduces the dependency problem at the consumption layer. |
89	| R3 | **Reuse the definition, never the instance.** | Consistency comes from a shared *meaning* in DAB, not from a shared *table* here. The conformed dimension buys agreement by sharing structure and pays in coupling; with a real integration layer beneath, that price is unnecessary. |
90	| R4 | **Volatile and generated.** Nothing here is hand-written or hand-edited. | Anything derived from DAB can be thrown away and rebuilt. An edit to generated output is lost on the next generation, and until then the code and the model quietly disagree. |
91	| R5 | **What was delivered, to whom, and when is recorded.** | An answer someone acted on must be reconstructable, including the definitions that produced it. |
92	
93	## What structure cannot do
94	
95	Generation guarantees **consistency**, not **correctness**. A poorly chosen model compiles just
96	as reliably as a good one, and a system that enforces coherent structure over incoherent
97	definitions produces coherent-looking incoherence — which is more dangerous than visible mess,
98	because it is trusted.
99	
100	Deciding what an entity is, when two records refer to the same instance, and whether two
101	attributes carry the same meaning remains human judgement. The effort saved on mechanism is meant
102	to be redirected to meaning, not removed.
103	
104	## No exceptions
105	
106	This document contains no exceptions and no pre-authorised bypass. That is deliberate: if a
107	principle is not stated as an absolute, with its reason recorded, there is nothing to break, and
108	a deviation becomes indistinguishable from an ordinary decision.
109	
110	Reality still wins sometimes. When it does, the answer is not to weaken the principle but to
111	**cost the deviation**: which principle breaks, why the conforming option was unworkable here,
112	what it costs, and the observable condition under which it is removed. That record lives in
113	[deviations.md](deviations.md), and every deviation has an ADR behind it.
114

1	# Deviations register
     2	
     3	Every knowing departure from a principle in [blueprint.md](blueprint.md) or a hard rule in
     4	[conventions.md](conventions.md) is recorded here, with the ADR that decided it.
     5	
     6	The register exists because an unregistered exception is indistinguishable from a mistake. Once
     7	one exists, the next person reads it as precedent and copies it, and a year later the rule is
     8	folklore. Writing the cost down keeps the trade visible; writing an exit condition down keeps it
     9	from becoming permanent by default.
    10	
    11	A deviation is legitimate only when all four fields are answerable. If the cost cannot be named,
    12	the deviation has not been understood. If the exit condition cannot be named, it is not a
    13	deviation but a change of rule, and the rule should be superseded instead.
    14	
    15	## Entries
    16	
    17	| # | Rule deviated from | Why | Cost | Exit condition | ADR | Status |
    18	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    19	| D-0001 | [blueprint.md](blueprint.md) **R2 — No cross-dependency**: "a data product owns its structures and does not consume another product's" | Every slice's page reads one generated Unified Star Schema in `dar__uss`. The structure being shared is additive by construction — keys inherit along many-to-one relationships, measures stay on the stage that owns them — so the fan trap R2 exists to prevent cannot occur in it, and one shared calendar is what lets two processes be compared at all. Generating a private copy per page would make that comparison a cross-schema join, which is most of what a USS is for | A change made for one reader is visible to all of them the moment it is generated. There is no per-reader projection, so "this reader may not see freight" cannot be expressed. Two readers cannot hold different definitions of the same measure. The first thing to break is a slice needing a measure defined one way for one reader and another way for another — it will have to be modelled as two measures | A second consumer needs isolation: a different shape of the same structure, or a group that must not see part of it. The generator then gains per-group projections over the same bridge and this entry is resolved | [0002](adr/0002-dar-is-one-generated-unified-star-schema.md) | open |
    20	
    21	## Entry format
    22	
    23	Entries are appended in the order they are decided and never removed. A resolved deviation is
    24	marked resolved, with the date and the commit or ADR that resolved it, because the history of why
    25	something looked necessary is worth as much as the fact that it no longer is.
    26	
    27	Field by field:
    28	
    29	* **Rule deviated from** — quote or link the exact rule. "The spirit of layering" is not a rule;
    30	  a row in a blueprint table is.
    31	* **Why** — the constraint that made the conforming option unworkable *here*. Convenience, time
    32	  pressure and unfamiliarity are not constraints; they are reasons to do it properly.
    33	* **Cost** — what this buys the system in trouble. Name the first thing that will break, who pays
    34	  for it, and which future change it makes more expensive. A deviation with no cost is evidence
    35	  the rule is wrong, so supersede the rule instead of deviating from it.
    36	* **Exit condition** — the observable thing that has to become true for the deviation to be
    37	  removed. "When we have time" is not observable.
    38	* **ADR** — the decision record that argued it. Every deviation has one; the register is the
    39	  index, the ADR is the argument.
    40	* **Status** — `open` while it stands, `resolved` once it is gone.
    41	
    42	## Review
    43	
    44	The register is read at the start of every slice. Each open entry is checked against its exit
    45	condition **and against whether its argument is still being carried on assertion** — D-0001's
    46	justification rests on measures not multiplying across a walk over many-to-one edges. Slice 2
    47	built the first edge, so the walk is now exercised; the property it is supposed to protect is
    48	not, because both entities on that edge are at the same grain and no measure *can* multiply
    49	across it. The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the
    50	argument stops being carried on assertion. ADR 0006 says the same in as many words. An entry should also be re-read the moment a second consumer appears, not only
    51	when isolation is demanded, because by then the shared structure will already have shaped both
    52	readers. An entry whose exit condition has been met and which is still open is a defect in the
    53	same way a failing test is: the system is no longer doing what its own documentation says.

1	     1	# Conventions
2	     2	
3	     3	The **one** convention document: naming, SQL style, YAML style, Python style, commit format.
4	     4	There is deliberately no second machine-readable copy of these rules. Where an off-the-shelf tool
5	     5	can already check a rule, **the tool's configuration is the rule** and this page records only the
6	     6	reason; everything else is checked by whoever — or whatever — reviews the change, reading this
7	     7	page.
8	     8	
9	     9	The reason is drift. A convention that exists both as prose and as a linter config exists twice,
10	    10	the two copies disagree within a quarter, and the disagreement is discovered by an argument in a
11	    11	pull request. One artefact means a clarification takes effect the moment it is written here.
12	    12	
13	    13	Principles live in [blueprint.md](blueprint.md); decisions in [adr/](adr/README.md); registered
14	    14	departures in [deviations.md](deviations.md).

16	    16	## How to read a rule
17	    17	
18	    18	Every rule carries a **why** and a severity. The why is not decoration: it is what lets a
19	    19	reviewer tell a genuine violation from a case the rule was never aimed at.
20	    20	
21	    21	| Severity | Meaning | On a pull request |
22	    22	|---|---|---|
23	    23	| **Hard rule** | Breaking it breaks a contract something else depends on. | Blocks. Fix it, or register a deviation with an ADR. |
24	    24	| **Guideline** | Judgement and taste. | A comment, not a block. A reasoned "no thanks" ends it. |

26	    26	## 1. Naming by layer
27	    27	
28	    28	Names are the interface between layers, so each layer names things in its own vocabulary and
29	    29	never in its neighbour's.
30	    30	
31	    31	The layers are called `das`, `dab` and `dar` literally — in schemas, in directories, in prose.
32	    32	Never bronze/silver/gold, never staging/core/marts. The name carries the principle
33	    33	([blueprint.md](blueprint.md)); a name that carries no principle cannot be enforced.
34	    34	
35	    35	### 1.1 DAS — the source-vocabulary exemption
36	    36	
37	    37	| Rule | Why | Severity |
38	    38	|---|---|---|
39	    39	| DAS object and column names mirror the source. The source's own words are **required** here, even where other layers forbid them. | DAS exists to say what the source said. Renaming a source field to a business term buries an interpretation in the layer that must make none. | Hard rule |
40	    40	| The mechanical translation is expected: a source property becomes `snake_case`, a source entity set becomes a `snake_case` plural table named after the source's own word for it. | A consistent spelling of the source's word is still the source's word. | Hard rule |
41	    41	| A contract file's stem is the landed table name, and that name is used in every schema of this layer. | One name for one thing, so grepping for a table finds its contract. | Hard rule |
42	    42	| A source name that would be a violation anywhere else — `ShipVia`, `total_orders` — is **not** a violation here. | It is a column in a table nobody on this side controls. A rule that cannot tell that case from a name we chose produces false accusations. | Hard rule |
43	    43	| A contract's `description` stays in system vocabulary: the source's type, its nullability, what the source calls it. Never what it means to the business. | Business meaning has exactly one home (§1.2). | Hard rule |
44	    44	| Columns this layer adds itself carry no source's word and are named for what they record: `payload`, `source_system`, `source_entity`, `source_url`, `extracted_at`, `extracted_on`. | Provenance is ours, not the source's, and must be tellable apart from it at a glance. | Hard rule |
45	    45	| A landed record is **one whole source record from one response**. Composing a landed row from more than one response is forbidden. | Blueprint S4 requires provenance per *data point*. One record per row makes a field's provenance the record's provenance — which is true only while that holds, and silently false the moment a row is composed from two responses. | Hard rule |
46	    46	| **No loader vocabulary crosses into `das__staged`.** `_dlt_load_id` and `_dlt_id` stay in `das__raw`; the staged view exposes `extracted_at` and `extracted_on`, derived from the load id, and nothing else of the loader's. | The blueprint's first promise is that every tool is replaceable without invalidating a principle. A loader's column name in the layer's published interface welds that loader in, in the layer everything else is rebuilt from. The derivation is injective, so no provenance is lost. | Hard rule |
47	    47	| A contract generates two staged objects: `das__staged.<table>`, the change log with one row per source record per load, and `das__staged.<table>__current`, one row per key from the latest load that carried it. | DAS is append-only (S2), so the change log is what it actually holds and is what DAB historizes from. `__current` exists because a question asked of the source needs one row per thing, not one per observation. | Hard rule |

49	    49	### 1.2 DAB — the business vocabulary
50	    50	
51	    51	| Rule | Why | Severity |
52	    52	|---|---|---|
53	    53	| Entity and attribute identifiers are `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`, with `id` and `name` holding the identical string. A **relationship** carries only a `name` — the modelling grammar has no `id` field for one — and its identifier is composed, `<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, per M6. | It is the modelling language's convention, and the visual break from every other layer's lower case makes a leak obvious on sight. | Hard rule |
54	    54	| Entity and attribute names are **singular**: `ORDER`, `ORDER_LINE`, `SHIP_COUNTRY`. | An entity names a kind of thing, not a pile of them. The pile is what a query produces. | Hard rule |
55	    55	| Descriptive attributes are prefixed with their entity (`CUSTOMER_NAME`, `ORDER_LINE_ID`); generic ones and measures are not (`STATUS`, `QUANTITY`). | The prefix is what makes an attribute readable once it has been inherited into a wide DAR row. | Guideline |
56	    56	| **No source name appears anywhere in `dab/model.yaml`** — not in an id, not in a name, not in a definition, not in a description. | This is the layer whose purpose is source-agnosticism; a source name in it means the dependency was moved rather than broken. | Hard rule |
57	    57	| Source names may appear in `dab/mappings/**`, and only in `table`, `primary_keys` and `transformation_expression`. | A mapping's entire job is to bind two vocabularies, and it cannot do that without naming both. Confining them to three keys is what keeps the binding auditable. | Hard rule |
58	    58	| `dab/uss.yaml` is governed by §1.3 and §2, not by this section. | It lives beside the model but it declares DAR things. One directory, two regimes; this sentence is the arbiter. | Hard rule |
59	    59	| Every entity, attribute and relationship has a `definition` in business language, and that is the **only** place the data is explained. | Everything else — contracts, questions, the generated layer, the app — references these. Two definitions eventually mean two numbers. | Hard rule |
60	    60	| A relationship name is a verb phrase, so `<SOURCE>_<NAME>_<TARGET>` reads as a sentence: `ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER`. | Direction is the thing people get wrong, and a sentence cannot be read backwards by accident. | Hard rule |

62	    62	| Prefer the word the business already uses over a more precise one it does not. | A model nobody recognises is a model nobody checks. | Guideline |

64	    64	### 1.3 DAR — the generated layer
65	    65	
66	    66	Names here are emitted by the generator, so these rules are what the generator implements. They
67	    67	are on this page because they are the contract every consumer is written against.
68	    68	
69	    69	| Rule | Why | Severity |
70	    70	|---|---|---|
71	    71	| Object names are `snake_case` **singular**, derived from the entity: `order`, `order_line`. A reserved word is quoted (`dar__uss."order"`), never abbreviated around. | Same reason as §1.2, in the other layer's spelling. Renaming to dodge a keyword breaks the mechanical link back to the concept. | Hard rule |
72	    72	| A key column is `<object>_key`. | One predictable spelling means a join can be written without looking anything up. | Hard rule |
73	    73	| Attribute columns are the lower-cased attribute identifier, unchanged. | The mapping back to its definition must be mechanical, so any column's meaning is one step away. | Hard rule |
74	    74	| Structural columns carry a leading underscore: `_bridge`, `_calendar`, `_stage`, `_event`, `_event_date`, `_is_current`, `_measure__…`. | The underscore says "the generator owns this". Anything without one came from the business model. | Hard rule |
75	    75	| The calendar's own columns are the exception, and carry none: `date_key`, `year_number`, `month_label`. | It is the one object the generator invents whole rather than deriving from the model, so there is no business name for its columns to be confused with, and these are the names a reader of any star schema already knows. | Hard rule |
76	    76	| Measure columns are `_measure__<entity>__<measure>`, where `<measure>` is the **whole** §2 name. `_measure__order__placed_orders_count`, not `_measure__order__placed`. | §2's payoff is searchability by any of the three parts, and that only holds if the whole name survives into the physical column. It costs long, repetitive column names; that is the price of the name being the same everywhere. | Hard rule |
77	    77	| The generator **never invents a member**. A null dimension stays null; there is no "Unknown" row, no "N/A" country, no placeholder date. | An invented member is meaning with no definition behind it, and §1.2 says meaning has exactly one home. A question that wants nulls grouped or excluded says so in the question file, where the choice belongs. | Hard rule |
78	    78	| The generator names every column it reads from a DAB view. It never selects `*` from `dab.*`. | daana's presentation views are themselves `SELECT *` over table macros, so a model change silently changes their shape. Naming the columns turns that into a regeneration diff. | Hard rule |
79	    79	| **Nothing in this layer is hand-edited.** A wrong name is fixed in the business model and regenerated. | Blueprint R4. An edit to generated output is lost on the next generation. | Hard rule |

81	    81	### 1.4 DAB — mapping rules
82	    82	
83	    83	A mapping says how one entity is loaded from DAS. These rules exist because daana accepts several
84	    84	kinds of wrong mapping without complaint, and two of them corrupt data silently.
85	    85	
86	    86	| # | Rule | Why | Severity |
87	    87	|---|---|---|---|
88	    88	| M1 | `table:` names a `das__staged` object and nothing else. Never a subquery, never a join, never `das__raw`. | Blueprint F3. A join here is business logic in the wrong layer; a raw read skips the contract's casts and the contract stops being the gate. | Hard rule |
89	    89	| M2 | Exactly **one** `primary_keys` entry, whose VARCHAR result is the entity key: a bare string column, `cast(col AS VARCHAR)`, or a `concat` of casts with a separator. | Two entries are two *alternate identifiers* to daana, not a composite key, and that mode cannot be undone once loaded. A `concat` without a separator makes `'A1' + '23'` and `'A12' + '3'` the same key. | Hard rule |
90	    90	| M3 | `ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG`. `FULL` is permitted only against a source view **proven** to hold exactly one row per key, and the proof is a data check, not a claim. | Observed: `FULL` against a multi-row-per-key source inserts one duplicate `_desc` row per execute, forever, and every presentation view hides it. Our staged change log is multi-row-per-key by construction, so `FULL` is the wrong default here and the failure is invisible. | Hard rule |
91	    91	| M4 | `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at`. | Blueprint B3. The effective time of a fact is when DAS observed it. Anything else dates the fact by something that is not about the fact — and no source here reports when it changed. | Hard rule |
92	    92	| M5 | An attribute expression reads its own row: a column, a cast, or **arithmetic over columns of that row** — including a same-row function such as `date_diff`. Never a subquery, never an aggregate, never a reach into another table. | An expression that reaches beyond the row is a join, and every join must come from a declared relationship. Arithmetic over one row produces a value the row already implies, so it needs no definition of its own beyond the attribute it lands in. | Hard rule |
93	    93	| M5a | What arithmetic does **not** cover: a `CASE`, a default, a coalesce that invents one, a filter, a bucket, or anything that changes the grain. Those go in the model as an attribute with a definition. | Each of them is a choice somebody made, and a choice needs a definition beside it. Every `CASE` is over columns *and* on their values, so listing it as permitted above and forbidden here decided nothing; by this rule's own test a `CASE` is always a choice. The mechanical check cannot tell arithmetic from a bucket — it is four keywords and seven function names — so this line is the rule and the regex is only its cheapest half. ADR 0007. | Hard rule |
94	    94	| M6 | A relationship's `id` is `<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`; its `source_table` is byte-identical to a `table` in its mapping; its target expression has the same **shape** as the target entity's own key expression — the same casts and the same functions, though the column may be named differently. Every edge the model declares is loaded by some mapping, and every edge a mapping loads is declared by the model. | A mismatched `source_table` is skipped silently, and a key of a different shape produces pairs that join to nothing. Neither says anything at load time. The shape is what matters and the spelling is not: a foreign key is routinely named differently from the primary key it points at, and it is the casting and the functions that decide the VARCHAR the two sides produce. | Hard rule |
95	    95	| M7 | Every mapped table carries at least one attribute. | daana refuses to deploy an entity with none, and the failure arrives at deploy rather than at review. | Hard rule |
96	    96	
97	    97	Start from the generated skeleton and replace **every** placeholder: they are all wrong on
98	    98	purpose, and all of them compile.

100	   100	## 2. Measure naming
101	   101	
102	   102	The most consequential convention here, and the one to get right first.
103	   103	
104	   104	**Pattern: `<descriptor>_<entities>_<unit>`.**
105	   105	
106	   106	| Rule | Why | Severity |
107	   107	|---|---|---|
108	   108	| Three parts in that order: what distinguishes it, the entity it counts or sums over, the unit it is in. | Three fixed slots make names comparable at a glance and searchable by any of the three. | Hard rule |
109	   109	| The entity part is **plural**: `orders`, `order_lines`. | A measure is always about a set. The singular is reserved for the entity itself. | Hard rule |
110	   110	| Scope and aggregation words never appear: no `total_`, `sum_`, `avg_`, `count_of_`, `num_`, `_ytd`, `_by_month`. | Aggregation and scope are chosen by the query, not baked into the name. `total_orders` is a lie the moment somebody filters it. | Hard rule |
111	   111	| The unit is a real unit: `count`, `amount`, `days`. | It is what tells a reader whether two measures can be added. | Hard rule |
112	   112	| **Ratios are not stored.** Store numerator and denominator as additive measures and divide at query time. | An average of averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at. | Hard rule |
113	   113	| A name must be self-explanatory without a glossary lookup, and must describe the business concept rather than the implementation. | If understanding a measure needs the glossary open, the name has failed at the only job a name has. | Guideline |
114	   114	| No abbreviations. `paid_subscriptions_count`, not `nbr_of_paid_subs`. | Abbreviations are unsearchable, and searchability is most of a name's value. | Guideline |
115	   115	
116	   116	| Instead of | Write | Because |
117	   117	|---|---|---|
118	   118	| `total_orders` | `placed_orders_count` | Scope word goes; the descriptor says *which* orders; the unit says what the number is. |
119	   119	| `sum_revenue` | `revenue_order_lines_amount` | `sum` is the query's job; the entity says at what grain revenue is measured. |
120	   120	| `avg_days_to_ship` | `ship_lag_orders_days` | The average is `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time, from two additive measures. |

122	   122	## 3. SQL style
123	   123	
124	   124	Everything a tool can check is checked by `sqlfluff` with [`.sqlfluff`](../.sqlfluff); this page
125	   125	records why the settings are what they are. All hard rules, because generated and hand-written
126	   126	SQL have to be indistinguishable to a reviewer.
127	   127	
128	   128	| Rule | Why |
129	   129	|---|---|
130	   130	| Dialect is `duckdb`. | Not a preference: the `postgres` dialect cannot parse `QUALIFY`. |
131	   131	| Keywords upper case, functions lower case, identifiers lower case. | Three visual classes, so structure, computation and data separate at a glance in a long generated statement. |
132	   132	| Four-space indent; one selected expression per line; every expression aliased with `AS`. | Diffs of generated SQL are read constantly. One expression per line makes a one-column change a one-line diff. |
133	   133	| Every table reference has an explicit alias, and a join condition names the earlier table first. | Reading order matches join order, so a wrong join key is visible without tracing back up the statement. |
134	   134	| `cast(x AS T)`, never `x::T`. | `CV11` enforces one casting style; `cast()` is the one that reads as a function like every other function. |
135	   135	| Every column reference in a multi-table statement is table-qualified. | `RF02`. It is the one rule sqlfluff cannot autofix, and it is a correctness rule, not a style one. |
136	   136	| Identifiers crossing over from DAB are double-quoted; everything this repository creates is lower case and unquoted, except reserved words. | The two conventions must be visually distinct, because a mixed-case identifier that loses its quotes fails only at run time. |
137	   137	| No `SELECT *` in anything a consumer reads, except a union of stages whose column list the generator fixes. | A star is a schema change waiting to be silent. |
138	   138	| SQL that lives in a Python string is written to a file so the same linter sees it. | A rule that applies only to the SQL somebody remembered to put in a `.sql` file is not a rule. |
139	   139	| Every `read_parquet` over the lake passes `union_by_name => true` and `hive_types` for the partition column. | Both are correctness, not taste. Without the first, a column that appears only in later loads is **silently dropped** — no error, just missing data. Without the second, the partition key comes back VARCHAR. |
140	   140	| Every path in a persisted view is absolute. | A relative path inside a view resolves against the process's working directory at **query** time, not at create time, so a view created from the repository root breaks the moment a page opens the same warehouse from elsewhere. |
141	   141	
142	   142	Four rules are excluded, and the reasons are in [`.sqlfluff`](../.sqlfluff): `AL09` forbids
143	   143	`x AS x`, which is exactly the every-column-aliased discipline that makes a `UNION` branch
144	   144	positionally safe; `RF06` fires on every mixed-case identifier crossing over from DAB; `LT05` and
145	   145	`LT09` are line-layout opinions a generator should not have to implement.

147	   147	## 4. YAML style
148	   148	
149	   149	Checked by `yamllint` with [`.yamllint.yaml`](../.yamllint.yaml).
150	   150	
151	   151	| Rule | Why | Severity |
152	   152	|---|---|---|
153	   153	| Two-space indent, no tabs, lines ≤ 160. | These files are read far more often than they are written. | Hard rule |
154	   154	| Flow mappings (`{a: 1, b: 2}`) are allowed for short homogeneous rows — a mapping attribute, a connection profile — but never column-aligned with padding spaces. A contract column has five keys and a prose description, so it is block style. | Alignment re-aligns the whole block the day one value grows, turning a one-line change into a twenty-line diff. | Hard rule |
155	   155	| Anything with an interpolation, a multi-line value, or more than about four keys is block style. | Flow style stops being readable exactly where the value stops being simple. | Hard rule |
156	   156	| Booleans are `true`/`false`. | One spelling. `yes`/`on` are the same value wearing a disguise. | Hard rule |

158	   158	## 5. Python style
159	   159	
160	   160	| Rule | Why | Severity |
161	   161	|---|---|---|
162	   162	| `ruff` with [`pyproject.toml`](../pyproject.toml) is the style. `ty --error all` is the type gate. | No style discussions, ever. | Hard rule |
163	   163	| `ANN` stays in the ruff selection. | `ty` does not flag a fully unannotated `def`. Without `ANN` the type gate has a hole. | Hard rule |
164	   164	| **No data vocabulary anywhere under `src/` or in test code.** No entity, attribute or business term from the model appears in the machinery or in a test. | The machinery must work for any source and any business model; a data name in it is proof that it does not. Test fixtures use neutral models held as data files, so the tests *prove* the machinery is generic rather than asserting it. | Hard rule |
165	   165	| Data vocabulary belongs in the YAML, SQL and Markdown artefacts — contracts, the model, generated SQL, questions, these documents. | Those artefacts *are* the description of this particular business. That is the point of keeping it out of the code. | Hard rule |
166	   166	| Names describe the machinery's concepts: `contract`, `pipeline`, `plan`, `stage`, `peripheral`, `question`, `destination`. | The machinery has its own domain and deserves its own vocabulary. | Guideline |
167	   167	| **No tool vocabulary in a published interface.** A tool's name may appear in the adapter that drives it and in that adapter's tests. It may not appear in a schema, a view's column, a generated artefact, or a CLI subcommand. | The blueprint's first promise is that every tool is replaceable. `adss das ingest`, not `adss dlt run`. | Hard rule |
168	   168	| marimo notebooks under `destinations/` are exempt from `ANN201` and are not formatted by `ruff format`. | A marimo cell is a decorated function whose return type is meaningless, and marimo rewrites the file itself on save, so a formatter fights it. The exemption is in the config, which §5 says *is* the rule. | Hard rule |

170	   170	## 6. Tests
171	   171	
172	   172	There are **two suites**, and they are not run at the same time or by the same thing.
173	   173	
174	   174	| Suite | What it is | When it runs |
175	   175	|---|---|---|
176	   176	| **machinery** (`tests/`) | Pure functions over data files. No warehouse, no network, no binary. | Every commit, by the pre-commit gate and by CI. |
177	   177	| **checks** (`checks/`) | Assertions about what the built warehouse actually contains. | After `adss build`, by CI and on demand. |
178	   178	
179	   179	The split is not fastidiousness. The warehouse is not committed, so a data check in the gate
180	   180	would fail in every fresh checkout — and §6's own rules forbid both of the ways out of that (a
181	   181	skip, or a stub to assert against). Naming the two suites is what lets "every commit is green"
182	   182	stay true.
183	   183	
184	   184	| Rule | Why | Severity |
185	   185	|---|---|---|
186	   186	| Machinery is test-first: the failing test and the code that passes it land in one commit. | A test written afterwards is a test that has only ever been seen to pass. | Hard rule |
187	   187	| A data check is never written against a stub or a fabricated warehouse. It asserts what the real build produced, and lands in the same commit as the build step that satisfies it. | TDD is for functions. A check that passes against a stub tells you nothing about the build. | Hard rule |
188	   188	| No `pytest.skip`, no imperative `xfail()` in a test body. | A skip is a test that silently does not exist. An imperative `xfail` can never report an unexpected pass, so it cannot tell you the day the bug is fixed. | Hard rule |
189	   189	| No test contains an entity, attribute, measure, source or column name from the business. Fixtures are neutral models held as **data files**; the question runner discovers question files and asserts over them without naming anything. | The machinery must work for any business; a business name in a test is proof that it does not. A per-question test *function* smuggles the vocabulary back in through its own name — so the runner is parameterised. | Hard rule |
190	   190	| A failing check is fixed by fixing the code, or by making the configuration honest. Never by weakening the test. | A weakened test costs the same to run and reports the opposite of the truth. | Hard rule |
191	   191	| **When a question's two queries disagree, `dab/model.yaml` is the arbiter.** The query that departs from the definition is the one that changes. Never adjust both until they match. | With two hand-written expressions of one question, "fix the code" is ambiguous by construction. Without a named arbiter, the cheapest repair is to make the check agree with itself, which deletes the only thing it was measuring. | Hard rule |

193	   193	## 7. Commits, branches and pull requests
194	   194	
195	   195	| Rule | Why | Severity |
196	   196	|---|---|---|
197	   197	| Conventional commits: `<type>(<scope>): <imperative>`. Types `feat`, `fix`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`, `refactor`, `ci`. Scopes: `repo`, `domain`, `das`, `dab`, `dar`, `questions`, `destination`, `ci`, `docs`, `adr`, `skills`. | The scope names the layer, so the history reads as a map of the architecture and a reviewer knows which rules apply before opening the diff. | Hard rule |
198	   198	| The subject is imperative, lower case, no trailing period, about 72 characters. | It is a heading, read in lists a hundred times more often than the body. | Guideline |
199	   199	| Every commit passes the gate and the whole suite on its own. | Bisect is only worth anything if every point in history is a working system. | Hard rule |
200	   200	| One business question per slice; one branch per slice, `claude/adss-slice-NN-<slug>`, branched off the previous slice. The slug is the **question's** slug, in the business's words. | The unit of delivery is an answered question, not a file — and a branch named in the source's vocabulary is the one artefact of the slice that disagrees with all the others. | Hard rule |
201	   201	| Stacked branches are rebased, never merged; pull requests are rebase-merged, never squashed. | Squashing destroys the trail that shows the question drove the change. Merge commits make a stack unreadable. | Hard rule |
202	   202	| An ADR lands before the code it decides. | A decision record written afterwards records what was built, not what was decided. | Hard rule |

205	   205	
206	   206	| Rule | Why | Severity |
207	   207	|---|---|---|
208	   208	| A decision goes in an ADR under [`adr/`](adr/README.md), numbered, in MADR format, and is superseded by a new file rather than edited. | The value of a decision record is the record of what was true when it was made. | Hard rule |
209	   209	| The first exception: a record may be corrected **within the slice that wrote it**, before any code depends on it, when an observation it rests on turns out to be false. Say so in the commit. | Superseding a record that was wrong before it was ever built on preserves nothing but the mistake, and leaves a reader two documents to reconcile where there was never a real decision to reverse. After that slice, supersede. | Hard rule |
210	   210	| The second exception: a record's **Confirmation** section is edited to match the checks that exist, at any time, and only ever to match them. | It is not a record of anything — it claims which checks exist *now*, so a stale one lies about the present rather than reporting the past. Twice it had drifted the other way, describing a check somebody meant to write. Every other section is history and is corrected in the record that found it wrong, quoted; ADR 0006 corrects two of ADR 0002's. | Hard rule |
211	   211	| A departure from a principle in [blueprint.md](blueprint.md) or a hard rule here needs an entry in [deviations.md](deviations.md) and an ADR. | An unregistered exception is indistinguishable from a mistake, and the next person copies it. | Hard rule |
212	   212	| Markdown lines stay around 100 characters, breaking at a sentence or clause — except table rows, which stay on one line. | Prose diffs stay legible; a re-wrapped paragraph should not look like a rewrite. | Guideline |
213	   213	| Prefer a table when there are three or more parallel things to say. | Parallel structure is easier to check for gaps than parallel prose. | Guideline |
214	   214	| Generated artefacts are **committed**, and a `--check` regeneration in the gate fails on any diff. The exception is an artefact that cannot be the same on two machines — DAS's view SQL embeds the lake's absolute path — which is generated at build time and gitignored, with the reason recorded where it is ignored. | Committing them makes what DAR served reviewable in a pull request. The drift check is what stops the committed copy becoming a second truth nothing compares against the model. Any formatting the generator's output needs must happen *inside* the generator, or every regeneration produces a spurious diff. | Hard rule |
215	   215	
216	   216	## 9. The warehouse has exactly one writer
217	   217	
218	   218	The lock is **per process**. Within one process every connection shares an instance, so a
219	   219	second open succeeds; across processes the second is refused. That distinction is the whole of
220	   220	this section, and getting it backwards costs an afternoon.
221	   221	
222	   222	| Rule | Why | Severity |
223	   223	|---|---|---|
224	   224	| This process must not hold the warehouse open while a separate process is asked to write to it. `require_detached` enforces it rather than asking anyone to remember. | The modelling engine is a separate process. While we hold the file it cannot take the lock, and it reports that as `daana framework is not installed on the remote database` — which is not what went wrong. Reproduced with DuckDB alone, no engine involved. | Hard rule |
225	   225	| Every destination opens the warehouse with `read_only=True`. | A read-only handle still holds the process lock, so a page left open blocks the next build; read-only at least keeps a reader from writing. | Hard rule |
226	   226	| `daana framework is not installed on the remote database` means **the file is busy**. | The real lock error is swallowed and does not appear even at debug level. Anyone meeting this message will otherwise spend an afternoon reinstalling a framework that is already installed. | Hard rule |
227	   227	
228	   228	## 10. Questions
229	   229	
230	   230	A question is the unit of delivery, and it is a **data file**, not code. That is what keeps the
231	   231	acceptance test free of business vocabulary (§6) and what lets the same artefact serve the test,
232	   232	the page and the reader.
233	   233	
234	   234	| Rule | Why | Severity |
235	   235	|---|---|---|
236	   236	| One directory per question under `docs/questions/NN-<slug>/`, holding `question.md` and the two SQL bodies as `.sql` files. | `.sql` files are linted by the same sqlfluff hook as everything else — §3 already demands that SQL not hide in a string. | Hard rule |
237	   237	| `question.md` front matter carries the measure, dimensions, aggregation, time grain, persona, status, and the definitions the question depends on. Its prose carries the story and the W's. | A question that needs a conversation to be answerable is a Stage 1 question, and the whole point is to reach Stage 3. | Hard rule |
238	   238	| A question **references** definitions; it never restates them. Every reference must resolve to something `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` defines, and the machinery proves it. | Blueprint B8. A restated definition is a second definition, and it will be the one that is out of date. | Hard rule |
239	   239	| A question that needs a term the model does not define is **blocked**, and the model change comes first. | This is the methodology working: a question the model cannot answer has found a gap in the model, which is what asking it was for. | Hard rule |
240	   240	| The staged query reads `das__staged.<table>__current` and must not mention `dab` or `dar__uss`. The USS query reads `dar__uss` only. Both halves are checked. | Independence is the whole value. A staged query that consults DAB is a transcription of the other one wearing a disguise; and the page runs the USS query verbatim, so one that reached past DAR would render, pass, and be exactly the invisible dependency the flow rules exist to prevent. | Hard rule |
241	   241	| The front matter's dimensions must appear in the **USS** query. They are DAR's names; the control query says the same thing in the source's words. | That difference is what makes the control independent rather than a transcription. Requiring the same spelling in both would force one to be written from the other. | Hard rule |
242	   242	
243	   243	## 11. When a rule does not fit
244	   244	
245	   245	Rules are aimed at cases; a case the rule was not aimed at is not a violation. Cheapest recourse
246	   246	first:
247	   247	
248	   248	1. **Clarify this page.** If the rule was ambiguous, say what it means and add the case. The
249	   249	   clarification is in force immediately, for everyone.
250	   250	2. **Register a deviation.** If the rule is right and this one place genuinely cannot follow it,
251	   251	   add an entry to [deviations.md](deviations.md) — rule, reason, cost, exit condition — and an
252	   252	   ADR explaining the decision.
253	   253	3. **Change the rule.** If it is wrong, supersede the ADR that established it and edit this page.
254	   254	   A rule nobody follows should be deleted rather than left as a reason to distrust the rest.
255	   255	
256	   256	What is not on the list: a quiet exception. That is how a system of conventions turns into a set
257	   257	of stories about why each file is the way it is.

     7	
     8	# Decisions are recorded as MADR files, written before the code they decide
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	This system is built for a life cycle measured in decades, and almost every difficult thing about
    13	it is a choice that had alternatives. Six months from now the question will not be "what does this
    14	code do" — that is readable — but "what else was considered, and what did we know at the time".
    15	
    16	Without a record, the answer is reconstructed from the code, which can only ever show the option
    17	that won. The alternatives, the constraint that ruled them out, and the cost that was knowingly
    18	accepted are all invisible, so the next person either re-litigates a settled question or, worse,
    19	quietly reverses it without knowing there was a decision there at all.
    20	
    21	## Decision Drivers
    22	
    23	* the reasoning has to outlive the person who did it
    24	* a reader must be able to tell a considered trade-off from an accident
    25	* a record must be cheap enough to write that it actually gets written
    26	* the record must be readable by an agent with no conversation history
    27	
    28	## Considered Options
    29	
    30	* MADR files in the repository, one per decision, written before the code
    31	* MADR files written after the implementation, describing what was built
    32	* Decisions recorded in pull request descriptions
    33	* Decisions recorded in an external wiki
    34	* No formal record; rely on commit messages
    35	
    36	## Decision Outcome
    37	
    38	Chosen option: **MADR files under `docs/adr/`, numbered, written before the code they decide.**
    39	
    40	Three properties make it the right one.
    41	
    42	*In the repository.* The decision travels with the code it governs, is reviewed in the same pull
    43	request, and is available to anyone — or anything — reading the repository with no other access.
    44	An external wiki is a second surface that drifts from the code, and a pull request description is
    45	unfindable six months later without knowing which pull request to open.
    46	
    47	*Before the code.* This is the part that does real work. Writing the options out before building
    48	forces the alternatives to be stated while they are still live, and it regularly changes the
    49	answer — which is the whole return on the exercise. A record written afterwards can only describe
    50	what was built, and its "considered options" section is reconstruction.
    51	
    52	*Superseded, never edited.* Editing a record to match current reality destroys the thing that
    53	made it worth keeping. A decision that has changed gets a new file that supersedes the old one, so
    54	both the old reasoning and the reason it stopped holding survive.
    55	
    56	The format is MADR because it names the parts that matter — context, drivers, options, outcome,
    57	consequences — and because "Consequences" is where the honest cost goes. A record with only good
    58	consequences has not been thought about.
    59	
    60	### Consequences
    61	
    62	* Good, because the reasoning behind every non-obvious choice is recoverable by anyone reading
    63	  the repository, with no conversation history and no access to the people involved
    64	* Good, because writing the alternatives down before building routinely changes what gets built
    65	* Good, because a decision and the code implementing it are reviewed together
    66	* Good, because [deviations.md](../deviations.md) has somewhere to point: the register is the
    67	  index, the ADR is the argument
    68	* Bad, because it is friction on every non-trivial change, and friction is what gets skipped under
    69	  deadline pressure. The mitigation is that the bar is "a decision that had alternatives", not
    70	  "every change" — a record for an obvious choice is noise that trains people to ignore the rest
    71	* Bad, because a superseded record left in place can be read as current by someone who does not
    72	  check the index or the `status` field
    73	
    74	### Confirmation
    75	
    76	The index in [README.md](README.md) lists every record. A pull request that changes an
    77	architectural choice without an accompanying record is incomplete, and that is a review check
    78	rather than an automated one — no linter can tell an architectural decision from a rename.
    79	---

    81	date: 2026-09-07
    82	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
