    85	
    86	# The machinery is modelled in its own typed vocabulary, and no business word appears under `src/`
    87	
    88	## Context and Problem Statement
    89	
    90	The brief asks for a domain model that does not restate `dab/model.yaml`. That constraint is
    91	easy to read as a style preference and it is not one: it decides what this repository is.
    92	
    93	There are two candidate domains here and they are genuinely different. One is the business —
    94	orders, countries, the dates on which things happened — and it already has a home, because
    95	`dab/model.yaml` is the only place the data is explained (blueprint B8). The other is the
    96	*system*: contracts, pipelines, landings, staged views, mappings, plans, stages, peripherals,
    97	bridges, questions, destinations. Nothing describes that domain yet, and it is the one the Python
    98	is actually about.
    99	
   100	The failure mode this guards against is specific. A pipeline that knows what an order is has
   101	stopped being a pipeline and become an order-loading script, and the next source needs a second
   102	one. The blog names this from the other direction: what makes a declarative platform work is that
   103	"an agent that learns the shape of one entity knows the shape of all of them"
   104	(*context-isnt-enough*). Uniformity is the property, and a special case in the machinery is what
   105	destroys it — quietly, one entity at a time.
   106	
   107	There is a real cost on the other side, and the same literature names it: over-generic models
   108	"lacking domain specificity" are one of the two named failure modes of model-driven platforms
   109	(*the-rise-of-model-driven-data-engineer*). A machinery vocabulary is a second thing to learn, and
   110	an abstraction built for slices that may never arrive is worse than the concrete code it replaced.
   111	
   112	## Decision Drivers
   113	
   114	* the machinery must work for a source and a business model it has never seen
   115	* the constraint must be checkable, not merely believed
   116	* tests must *prove* the machinery is generic rather than assert it
   117	* the model must be small enough that slice 1 does not pay for slice 6
   118	
   119	## Considered Options
   120	
   121	* A typed machinery domain model, with no business vocabulary under `src/` or in tests
   122	* Untyped dictionaries and strings throughout, with the shape documented in prose
   123	* A machinery model that names business concepts where it is convenient
   124	* A generic model built now for all six slices
   125	
   126	## Decision Outcome
   127	
   128	Chosen option: **a typed machinery domain model with no business vocabulary under `src/` or in
   129	tests**, and neutral fixture systems held as data files.
   130	
   131	The rule earns its keep by being falsifiable. "The machinery is generic" is an assertion; "no
   132	business word appears in it" is a property anyone can check by reading, and a reviewer who finds
   133	`order` in a function name has found a real defect without needing to understand the pipeline. It
   134	converts an architectural intention into something a code review can act on.
   135	
   136	Tests are where the rule does its most useful work. A test that loads a fixture called `ORDER`
   137	proves the machinery works for orders; a test that loads a neutral fixture — `PARENT`, `CHILD`,
   138	declared in a YAML file the test does not read for meaning — proves it works for *a* model. The
   139	second is the claim we actually want, and it is only available if the vocabulary stays out of the
   140	test. This is also why the question runner is parameterised over discovered question files rather
   141	than written as one test function per question: a per-question function smuggles the business
   142	vocabulary back in through its own name.
   143	
   144	Untyped dictionaries were the serious alternative, and they lose on the same ground. The types are
   145	where the machinery's own concepts are *named*, and a `dict[str, Any]` passed between six
   146	functions has no domain model at all — only a convention nobody can check. A strict type checker
   147	handles frozen dataclasses, string enums and discriminated unions with no friction, so the cost of
   148	typing is close to zero and the return is a compiler that refuses to let a `Contract` be used
   149	where a `Model` is meant.
   150	
   151	The last option — building the model for all six slices now — is rejected on the named failure
   152	mode. Slice 1 gets exactly the types slice 1 needs. No `Relationship`, no `Cardinality`, no
   153	measure kinds, no dialect abstraction beyond the single seam. Every one of those arrives in the
   154	slice that first has two of something to generalise over, which is the only point at which the
   155	generalisation can be judged.
   156	
   157	### Consequences
   158	
   159	* Good, because the claim "this works for any source and any business model" becomes a property a
   160	  reader can verify rather than a promise
   161	* Good, because the types name the machinery's own domain, which is otherwise nameless and lives
   162	  only in whoever wrote the pipeline
   163	* Good, because a neutral fixture makes a test prove genericity instead of asserting it
   164	* Bad, because there is now a second vocabulary to learn, and someone debugging a data problem has
   165	  to translate between "peripheral" and the entity they were actually looking at
   166	* Bad, because the rule has an awkward edge at the boundary: SQL generation must *emit* business
   167	  names it may not *contain*, so those names arrive as data and the code manipulating them reads
   168	  more abstractly than the thing it produces
   169	* Bad, because building only for slice 1 guarantees refactoring in slices 2 and 4, when
   170	  relationships and a second grain arrive. That is the intended trade: refactoring under a test
   171	  suite is cheaper than an abstraction chosen before the second case existed
   172	
   173	### Confirmation
   174	
   175	`tests/` contains no entity, attribute, measure, source or column name from the business, and its
   176	fixtures are neutral models held as data files. That is a hard rule in
   177	[conventions.md §5 and §6](../conventions.md) and it is checked by reading — no linter can tell a
   178	business noun from a machinery one, and a regex list of forbidden words would be a second copy of
   179	the business model living in the machinery, which is the thing this record forbids.
   180	
   181	The type gate is `ty --error all`, and `ANN` stays in the ruff selection because `ty` does not
   182	flag a fully unannotated `def`.

     7	
     8	# DAR is one generated Unified Star Schema: an event bridge whose stages own their measures and inherit only keys, one peripheral per entity, one dense calendar
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	DAR is the layer a person reads. The blueprint says it is volatile and generated (R4), and the
    13	Unified Star Schema is the shape chosen for it: one *bridge* holding a row per measurement event,
    14	one *peripheral* per entity holding its current state, and one calendar every process is dated
    15	against. This record fixes what the generator emits, because every question, every page and every
    16	future consumer is written against those column names and will not survive them changing.
    17	
    18	Three things about the source make the shape less obvious than the description sounds.
    19	
    20	**Fan-out.** The USS description says keys and measures propagate downward along many-to-one
    21	relationships. Keys can. Measures cannot: if a parent's measure were copied onto every child row
    22	that points at it, summing that measure would multiply it by the number of children. That is the
    23	classic fan trap, and avoiding it is the entire reason a bridge exists rather than one wide join.
    24	
    25	**History.** DAB keeps a version of every entity row. A question about something that *happened*
    26	and a question about a state as it was *observed* are different questions and need different rows,
    27	but they belong in one table, because the whole value of the bridge is that two processes can be
    28	summed and compared on one calendar.
    29	
    30	**What the generator is allowed to read.** Two observations constrain this hard, and both were
    31	made against the real engine on DuckDB rather than reasoned about. `<entity>_focal` and
    32	`<entity>_idfr` are created but never populated — a generator that joined to them would produce
    33	empty results and no error. And `view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship key columns at
    34	all, despite its name; its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`. A generator built on
    35	the names alone would be wrong in both directions.
    36	
    37	There is a fourth thing, and it is the one this slice cannot demonstrate. The argument that one
    38	shared bridge is safe rests on the walk over many-to-one edges. Slice 1 has one entity and no
    39	relationships, so the walk has zero edges and nothing inherits. The property is asserted here and
    40	first exercised in slice 2.
    41	
    42	## Decision Drivers
    43	
    44	* a `sum()` over the bridge is right without the reader knowing how the model is shaped
    45	* one calendar, so two processes can be compared
    46	* a published column contract that a model change *extends* rather than rearranges
    47	* deterministic output: the same declarations always produce the same SQL
    48	* nothing silently missing
    49	
    50	## Considered Options
    51	
    52	* An event bridge with one stage per (entity, event), keys inherited and measures owned
    53	* One bridge row per entity instance, with measures joined on
    54	* A hand-written star schema per question
    55	* Reading DAB's relationship views for the inherited keys
    56	
    57	## Decision Outcome
    58	
    59	Chosen option: **an event-grained bridge whose stages own their measures and inherit only keys.**
    60	
    61	*Keys inherit; measures do not.* A stage carries the key of every entity it reaches by walking
    62	many-to-one edges, and a measure is non-null only on the stage of the (entity, event) that owns
    63	it. Every other branch of the union emits a typed `NULL` in that column. This is what makes
    64	`sum()` additive at any grain the reader chooses, and it is proved by a test rather than trusted:
    65	a fixture with two parents and three children, where `sum(_measure__parent__…)` must still be the
    66	parent total and not three times it.
    67	
    68	*One row per measurement event.* A transaction stage reads `dab.view_<E>_hist`, keeps the latest
    69	version in which the event's date is set, and dates the row by that attribute. An unshipped order
    70	therefore has no shipment event *by construction* rather than by a filter somebody has to
    71	remember. A state stage reads the same history view, dates rows by `eff_tmstp`, and marks the
    72	latest version per key `_is_current`. Both kinds land in the same table with the same columns,
    73	which is what lets them be compared.
    74	
    75	*The generator reads `view_<entity>_hist` and the relationship pair objects, and nothing else.*
    76	Not `_focal`, which is empty. Not `_with_rel`, which does not carry what its name implies. Reading
    77	the current view instead of the history view would also lose `_observed_at`, which is how a bridge
    78	row carries its own provenance back to the DAS load that produced it.
    79	
    80	The rejected options each fail on one of the drivers. One row per entity instance with measures
    81	joined on is the fan trap, restated as a design. A hand-written star per question abandons R4 and
    82	puts the layer's correctness in a person's hands, every time, forever. Reading the relationship
    83	*views* rather than the pair objects is the subtle one: those views rank pairs by effective
    84	timestamp and keep the open rows, and our effective timestamp is the moment DAS observed the row,
    85	so a changed foreign key can drop out of the view entirely — rows silently missing from the
    86	bridge, with the query still running and the total merely smaller.
    87	
    88	### The column contract
    89	
    90	`dar__uss._bridge`:
    91	
    92	| column | type | null | meaning |
    93	|---|---|---|---|
    94	| `_stage` | VARCHAR | no | the entity this row is a row *of* |
    95	| `_event` | VARCHAR | no | the event, lower-cased: `placed`, `shipped`, `observed` |
    96	| `_event_date` | DATE | no | the day it happened, or the day the state was observed; joins `_calendar.date_key` |
    97	| `_is_current` | BOOLEAN | no | always true on a transaction stage; the latest version per key on a state stage |
    98	| `_observed_at` | TIMESTAMP | no | the DAB `eff_tmstp` behind this row, which is the DAS `extracted_at` |
    99	| `<entity>_key` | VARCHAR | own key no, inherited yes | one per entity in model order |
   100	| `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` | BIGINT for a count, DECIMAL(28,8) for a sum | non-null only on the owning stage | one per declared measure, in model order |
   101	
   102	`dar__uss.<entity>` is a peripheral **table**, one row per key, key first and attributes in
   103	declaration order. Tables rather than views, so what DAR served is exactly what the build log
   104	describes.
   105	
   106	`dar__uss._calendar` is dense and daily from the first to the last `_event_date` in the bridge,
   107	with civil arithmetic only — `year_number`, `quarter_of_year`, `month_of_year`, `day_of_month`,
   108	`year_start`, `quarter_start`, `month_start`, `quarter_label`, `month_label`. Column names avoid
   109	reserved words. Fiscal periods and holidays are business meaning and would need a definition, so
   110	they belong in DAB and not in a generator.
   111	
   112	Two rules follow from the contract and are written down because they are query-time traps: a join
   113	on the row's own stage key may be `INNER`, a join on an inherited key must be `LEFT`; and a ratio
   114	is `sum(a) / sum(b)` at query time, never a stored measure.
   115	
   116	Nulls: the generator never invents a member. A null dimension stays null, and a question that
   117	wants nulls grouped or excluded says so in the question file, where that choice belongs.
   118	
   119	### Consequences
   120	
   121	* Good, because a sum over the bridge is additive whatever the shape of the model, and the proof
   122	  is a test rather than a convention
   123	* Good, because every process lands on one calendar, so two of them can be compared
   124	* Good, because a consumer writes against a contract that a model change extends — new entities
   125	  and measures are appended, never inserted or renamed
   126	* Good, because a changed foreign key keeps its row, which reading the relationship view would not
   127	  have done
   128	* Bad, because the bridge is sparse: most cells of most rows are null. At this scale that costs
   129	  nothing, and it is the price of one table instead of one per process
   130	* Bad, because ratios and state questions need care at query time, and nothing in the schema stops
   131	  a reader averaging an average
   132	* Bad, because this slice cannot demonstrate the property the shared-bridge deviation (D-0001)
   133	  rests on. With one entity there are no edges to inherit along, so the fan-trap argument is
   134	  carried on assertion until slice 2
   135	* Bad, because the generator now depends on three specific behaviours of a third-party engine on a
   136	  platform that engine does not advertise supporting. Each is pinned by a check, but a vendor
   137	  change could invalidate any of them
   138	
   139	### Confirmation
   140	
   141	A machinery test asserts the column order, the event-date filter and the refusals — including
   142	that a **zero-edge walk is a valid walk**, so slice 2 does not meet that as a special case. A
   143	second asserts that every branch of the union emits the contract columns **in the contract
   144	order**, which is stronger than aliasing each once and is the assertion that matters: a union
   145	takes its column names from its first branch, so a branch that emits the right columns in a
   146	different order puts one measure's values silently into another measure's column, and `DESCRIBE`
   147	still matches. Every emitter's output, laid out the way the generator lays it out, is run through
   148	the repository's own linter.
   149	
   150	Data checks pin the engine behaviours this design rests on, so a vendor change says so rather
   151	than quietly emptying the star schema: that `_focal` and `_idfr` are still empty; that
   152	`view_<E>_with_rel` is still a passthrough on a relationship's *source* side and gains exactly
   153	the source entity's columns on its *target* side; and that `v_<edge>` still hands over the raw,
   154	unranked pairs. The `with_rel` check first asserted the passthrough of *every* entity, which was
   155	true only while there were no relationships — ADR 0006 corrects the observation, and this
   156	section now describes the check that exists. A fourth asserts `DESCRIBE dar__uss._bridge`
   157	equals the plan on the real warehouse, and a fifth counts the description table directly, which is
   158	the only place an ingestion-strategy defect is visible.
   159	
   160	**The fan-out test is not among them, and cannot be yet.** It needs two grains — parents and
   161	children — and this slice has one entity. It lands with the second grain, in the slice that first
   162	creates something for a measure to multiply across. Until then the property is argued rather than
   163	demonstrated, which [deviations.md](../deviations.md) records against D-0001 as well.
   164	
   165	`adss dar generate --check` regenerates and fails on any diff, which is what keeps the committed
   166	SQL from becoming a second truth.
   167	
   168	This decision is the argument behind deviation **D-0001** in
   169	[deviations.md](../deviations.md).

1	---
     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-07
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 2
     6	---
     7	
     8	# An inherited key is resolved from the raw pairs, as of the observation time of the row that inherits it
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	Slice 1 built a bridge with one entity and no relationships. ADR 0002 asserted that one shared
    13	bridge is safe because keys inherit along many-to-one edges while measures do not, and said in as
    14	many words that the walk had zero edges and the property was asserted rather than exercised. This
    15	slice is the first with an edge: an order is placed by a customer, and the question groups the
    16	freight of an order by the *customer's* country, which exists nowhere on the order.
    17	
    18	So the generator has to get `customer_key` onto an order row. The engine offers four places to get
    19	it from, they do not agree with each other, and the names do not say which is which. A probe built
    20	a two-entity model with one relationship, changed a foreign key, and read every object the engine
    21	produced. It overturned two things ADR 0002 states as fact.
    22	
    23	**The relationship view is a *current* view, not a historical one.** ADR 0002 says reading it would
    24	lose a row whose foreign key changed. That is not what happens. The macro behind
    25	`dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is:
    26	
    27	```sql
    28	rank() OVER (PARTITION BY <SRC>_key, type_key ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC) AS nbr
    29	... WHERE nbr = 1 AND row_st = 'Y'
    30	```
    31	
    32	Partitioned by the child, so the child never drops out — it is re-pointed. After the probe moved
    33	CH1 from P1 to P2, the pair table held both rows with `row_st = 'Y'` and the view held `CH1|P2`
    34	alone. Nothing is lost; the *old* pair is what is lost, for every row of that child, retroactively.
    35	The reason to read the raw pairs is therefore history, not disappearance, and ADR 0002 got the
    36	right answer from the wrong mechanism.
    37	
    38	**`view_<entity>_with_rel` does carry relationship keys — on the target side, and it fans out.**
    39	ADR 0002 says its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`. That is true only for the
    40	relationship's *source* entity. Once an entity is a relationship *target*, its `_with_rel` view
    41	becomes a double left join through the pair macro and gains the source entity's key **and every one
    42	of its attributes**, one row per child. The probe measured the consequence:
    43	`sum(CHILD_AMOUNT)` over `view_PARENT_with_rel` returned 200.75 against a true 150.75. That is a
    44	live fan trap in a view whose name invites exactly the join that springs it.
    45	
    46	**`rank()` is not `row_number()`, so a tie returns both rows.** The probe's CH5 had two parent codes
    47	in one load, so two pair rows shared an `eff_tmstp`, and the relationship view returned CH5 twice.
    48	A child appearing twice in the bridge multiplies its measures — the precise failure the bridge
    49	exists to prevent, arriving from the engine's own view rather than from anything we wrote.
    50	
    51	**The model cannot say that an edge is many-to-one.** This is the finding that decides how the rule
    52	is enforced, and it is settled by the engine's own error rather than inferred: adding
    53	`cardinality:` to a relationship is rejected with *"Valid fields are: name, definition, description,
    54	source, target, source_entity_id, target_entity_id, type"*, and that list is the whole grammar. The
    55	one candidate, `type`, is not a cardinality slot — it accepts any string without validation
    56	(`1:N`, `MANY_TO_ONE`, `BOGUS_VALUE` all pass `check model`) and is **dropped on compile**: it does
    57	not appear in the compiled `model.json` and never reaches the engine. Nor is the engine merely
    58	silent about cardinality. It is agnostic by design: it treats a child's parents as a *set*,
    59	aggregating all target keys per `(source key, eff_tmstp)` into a fingerprint and writing a row when
    60	that set changes. Many-to-many is a supported case, not a defect.
    61	
    62	So the generator cannot learn "many-to-one" from the model, and it cannot learn it from the data,
    63	because the data is legitimately allowed to be many-to-many. Something else has to say it.
    64	
    65	## Decision Drivers
    66	
    67	* a measure summed over the bridge is additive at every grain, whatever the model's shape
    68	* a bridge row is true as of one instant, and every column on it is true as of that same instant
    69	* the generator reads objects whose behaviour has been observed, never ones whose names suggest it
    70	* a case the design cannot handle fails the build loudly rather than answering a question wrongly
    71	* the walk works for zero edges, one edge and, later, a chain — without a special case per depth
    72	
    73	## Considered Options
    74	
    75	* `dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the engine's ranked relationship view
    76	* `dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the raw pairs plus a relationship name, ranked here
    77	* `dab.<SRC>_<TGT>_x` — the pair table directly, with `dab__meta` for the type key
    78	* `dab.view_<TGT>_with_rel` — the view named as though it were for this
    79	
    80	## Decision Outcome
    81	
    82	Chosen option: **`dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, ranked in the generated SQL as of the child row's own
    83	`_observed_at`, one parent per child, with the tie refused by a data check.**
    84	
    85	`v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is the raw pair table joined to the engine's metadata to add a `rel_name`
    86	column, with no ranking and no `row_st` filter. That is what makes it the right source: the pairs
    87	arrive unfiltered, and the as-of rule is ours and visible in the generated SQL rather than the
    88	vendor's and hidden in a macro. It also solves a naming problem the pair table has on its own — the
    89	pair table is named `<SRC>_<TGT>_x` from the *entity pair*, not from the relationship, so two
    90	relationships between the same two entities land in one table separated only by a `type_key` whose
    91	meaning lives in `dab__meta.atom_contx_desc`. Filtering on `rel_name` says what is meant; filtering
    92	on `type_key = 1` says nothing and breaks when a second edge is declared.
    93	
    94	**As of `_observed_at`, not as of now.** The stage picks a version of the child; the inherited key
    95	is the one in force when that version was observed. Today the stage always picks the child's latest
    96	version, so this coincides with the current parent and the choice looks free. It is not: it is what
    97	keeps the rule stated at the level of a bridge row rather than at the level of a table, so it
    98	survives a stage that keeps more than the latest version, which is what a snapshot event and a
    99	`_is_current = FALSE` row will both need.
   100	
   101	So the ranking partitions by the inheriting key **and its observation time**, not by the key
   102	alone. A review of this slice caught the first draft doing the latter, which collapses to one
   103	parent per key and would hand every retained version of an entity that same parent — "as of now"
   104	wearing this rule's clothes, and passing every check because today no stage keeps two versions.
   105	The distinction costs one column in a `PARTITION BY` and is the entire difference between the
   106	option chosen here and the one rejected.
   107	
   108	**Exactly one parent per child, and a tie is a build failure.** Since neither the model nor the data
   109	can state the cardinality, it is inferred from the mapping and then pinned. The inference is sound:
   110	M5 already forbids an attribute expression from containing a subquery, an aggregate or a reach into
   111	another table, so a relationship's `target_transformation_expression` reads its own row and is
   112	single-valued per staged row *by construction*. What that does not cover is one key appearing on
   113	several staged rows of a single load, which is exactly how the probe's CH5 acquired two parents at
   114	one instant. So the check is not optional decoration on top of the inference — it is the half of the
   115	argument the inference cannot make.
   116	
   117	The generated SQL uses `row_number()` over `eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC` and then the parent key
   118	itself, so it is deterministic and can never emit two rows for one child. `ver_tmstp` is not a
   119	formality: the engine writes a closing row that shares its predecessor's `eff_tmstp` and is
   120	separated from it only by `ver_tmstp`. Determinism alone would be a silent wrong answer, so a
   121	generated check counts children with more than one open parent at the ranking instant and fails the
   122	build when it is not zero. The two together mean the bad case is loud, and that if the check is ever
   123	ignored the damage is a mis-attributed row rather than a doubled measure. Doubling is worse: it is
   124	invisible in both of a question's acceptance queries if both are written the same way.
   125	
   126	**Only open pairs.** The read filters `row_st = 'Y'`. The engine flips a pair to `'N'` in exactly one
   127	case — the source row disappears from `das__staged`, and `FULL_LOG`'s delete branch closes it — and
   128	it keeps both rows when it does. In this architecture `das__staged` is an append-only view over
   129	parquet, so that should never fire; the filter is there because "should never fire" is not a reason
   130	to read a retracted pair if it ever does.
   131	
   132	`view_<TGT>_with_rel` is refused outright and now for a measured reason rather than an assumed one.
   133	The engine's ranked view is refused because its as-of rule is not ours to state and its `rank()`
   134	can fan out. The pair table is refused because it cannot name the relationship it is carrying.
   135	
   136	**A child with no parent keeps its row and inherits a null key.** The probe's CH6 has no pair row at
   137	all, so the join is a left join. An order the source attributes to nobody is still an order that
   138	was placed, and dropping it would change a count that ADR 0002 already published. Null is not a
   139	member: it groups as itself and the generator invents nothing for it, per conventions §1.3.
   140	
   141	### Corrections to ADR 0002
   142	
   143	ADR 0002 is not superseded — its decision stands and this record extends it. Two of its factual
   144	claims are wrong and are corrected here rather than in place, because what a record was when it was
   145	made is the thing that makes it worth keeping:
   146	
   147	1. "A changed foreign key keeps its row, which reading the relationship view would not have done."
   148	   The relationship view does keep the row. It re-points every one of that child's rows at the new
   149	   parent and erases the old pair, which is a different defect and a worse one, because it is
   150	   invisible.
   151	2. "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship key columns at all; its column list is
   152	   byte-identical to `view_<entity>`." True on the source side only. On the target side it carries
   153	   the source entity's key and attributes, fanned out. **ADR 0004 repeats the same claim** —
   154	   "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship keys despite its name" — and is corrected
   155	   here too, not there.
   156	
   157	A third claim, in this record's own first draft, was corrected a commit later: it was written
   158	from a partial reading of the probe that produced it. What that cost is worth naming, because it
   159	is the failure mode this whole arrangement is meant to catch — the decision it reached was the
   160	one the full report supports, so nothing downstream was wrong, and it was right by luck rather
   161	than by reading. The findings it had missed changed how the decision is *enforced*, not what it
   162	is.
   163	
   164	The check ADR 0002 installed for the second claim asserted it of *every* entity, so it fails the
   165	moment CUSTOMER becomes a relationship target. That is the check working: it was pinning observed
   166	behaviour and the behaviour was mis-observed. It is replaced by one that asserts the real rule —
   167	the source side is unchanged, the target side gains exactly the source entity's columns — which is
   168	a stronger statement than the one it replaces and would have caught this in slice 1 had it been
   169	possible to write then.
   170	
   171	## Consequences
   172	
   173	* Good, because the as-of rule is written in the generated SQL, so a reader of `dar/uss/_bridge.sql`
   174	  can see when the inherited key was true without reading a vendor macro
   175	* Good, because the fan-out the engine's own views expose cannot reach the bridge: the generator
   176	  emits `row_number()`, and the case that would have needed it fails the build first
   177	* Good, because filtering on `rel_name` keeps two edges between the same two entities in
   178	  separate pair objects. It does **not** keep them apart in the bridge, which a review of this
   179	  slice caught: a stage carries one key column per entity it inherits from, so two such edges —
   180	  or an edge from an entity to itself — would emit that column twice under one name, and DuckDB
   181	  resolves the ambiguity instead of raising. The generator refuses both shapes rather than
   182	  emitting them. Naming the column after the edge instead of the target would allow them and
   183	  would change the bridge's published contract, so it is a decision for the slice that first
   184	  needs two, not a shape to guess at now
   185	* Good, because the walk is the same shape at zero edges and one, so slice 5's two-hop chain extends
   186	  it rather than special-cases it
   187	* Bad, because the generated bridge SQL grows a ranked CTE per edge, and at three or four edges it
   188	  stops being readable in one screen. It is generated, linted and drift-checked, so this costs
   189	  legibility rather than correctness
   190	* Bad, because `v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is an engine-internal object with no compatibility promise,
   191	  like every other object here. The pinning checks are what turn a vendor change into a failure
   192	  instead of an empty column
   193	* Bad, and not fixable here: **a foreign key set to null is never retracted.** The engine's reader
   194	  filters the pair source on the target key being non-null, so "this child now belongs to nobody" is
   195	  inexpressible — re-landing a child with a null parent writes no row, no tombstone and no `row_st`
   196	  flip, and the stale pair survives forever. The probe reproduced this. If the source ever nulls an
   197	  order's customer, DAB keeps the old customer and nothing says so. That is a property of the
   198	  engine, not of this decision; it is recorded here because this is the decision that would
   199	  otherwise be blamed for it
   200	
   201	## More Information
   202	
   203	The probe found one thing that is not used and should be, when there is a reason to. Every
   204	presentation object wraps a DuckDB table macro taking a `p_eff_tmstp` with a default, so the whole
   205	DAB layer is point-in-time queryable for nothing: `f_child_parent_x(TIMESTAMP '2026-01-15')` returned
   206	the January parent while `f_child_parent_x()` returned the current one. That is a second, shorter
   207	way to write the as-of join. It is not taken because it moves the as-of rule back inside a vendor
   208	macro, which is the thing this decision is spending SQL to avoid — but a later slice that needs
   209	as-of over several objects at once should weigh it again rather than rediscover it.
   210	
   211	`type_key` is not stable across models: it was 1 for the relationship in this probe and 17 in an
   212	earlier one, and attribute type keys differ per entity within a single model. It is never
   213	hardcoded — `rel_name` is what the generated SQL matches on, which is the whole reason
   214	`v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is read rather than the pair table it wraps.
   215	
   216	## Confirmation
   217	
   218	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts the generated bridge left-joins the pairs rather than inner-joining
   219	them, that it ranks by `row_number` and not `rank`, that the ranking is as of the child's
   220	`_observed_at`, and that a non-owning branch still emits a typed null for a key it does not own —
   221	this last one because a union takes its column names from its first branch, so the order of the key
   222	columns is the invariant and counting them would not catch a transposition.
   223	
   224	A generated data check counts children with more than one parent at the ranking instant and must
   225	return zero. Another counts bridge rows whose inherited key resolves to no row in the target
   226	peripheral, which is the shape a mis-spelled M6 target expression takes: the engine reports nothing
   227	at deploy or at execute, and the column is simply null everywhere.
   228	
   229	The engine-behaviour checks are widened rather than removed: `_focal` and `_idfr` are still empty,
   230	`view_<E>_with_rel` is unchanged on a relationship's source side and gains exactly the source
   231	entity's columns on its target side.
   232	
   233	What this slice still does not prove is the fan-out property itself. Both entities here are at the
   234	same grain — one order has one customer — so no measure can multiply across the edge no matter how
   235	the join is written. The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the
   236	test that a parent's measure is not multiplied by its children becomes possible. Saying so is the
   237	point: ADR 0002 asserted this property in slice 1 and it is still asserted now.

1	---
     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-08
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 3
     6	---
     7	
     8	# A value derived from one row is modelled in DAB and computed in the mapping, and arithmetic there is bounded by this record
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	"How many days did they take" is the first number this system reports that does not exist in the
    13	source. Every measure so far has been a count — one per row — or a sum of a single attribute that
    14	was already there. A ship lag is two dates subtracted, and there is no established place to put
    15	the subtraction.
    16	
    17	Three things are already settled and an argument that reopens them has not read the standard.
    18	
    19	**The measure's name and its arithmetic are written down.** Conventions §2's own worked example is
    20	this question:
    21	
    22	> | `avg_days_to_ship` | `ship_lag_orders_days` | The average is
    23	> `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time, from two additive
    24	> measures. |
    25	
    26	So the two measures are named, the division is a question's job, and `ship_lag_orders_days` is a
    27	*stored measure* — a column in the bridge's published contract. That sentence decides more of this
    28	slice than anything else in the repository.
    29	
    30	**An event that did not happen is already decided.** ADR 0002: "A transaction stage reads
    31	`dab.view_<E>_hist`, keeps the latest version in which the event's date is set… An unshipped order
    32	therefore has no shipment event *by construction* rather than by a filter somebody has to
    33	remember." The generator emits `WHERE <date> IS NOT NULL` and a test pins it. The 21 unshipped
    34	orders are the case that design was written for, not a new problem.
    35	
    36	**Two events on one entity already work.** The neutral fixture has declared two events on one
    37	entity since slice 1, and generating this slice's bridge from a scratch copy of the model needs
    38	**no generator change at all**. What is new is one thing only: a sum measure with no attribute to
    39	point at.
    40	
    41	## Decision Drivers
    42	
    43	* a number the business reads has exactly one definition, in the one place data is explained
    44	* the acceptance check keeps an arbiter: when two queries disagree, something decides which is wrong
    45	* the precedent this sets is one the next three slices can live with
    46	* a rule the next person inherits, rather than an example they have to interpret
    47	* DAR stays a layer that can be deleted and rebuilt from the model
    48	
    49	## Considered Options
    50	
    51	* **(a)** A `NUMBER` attribute on `ORDER`, computed in the mapping from two columns of its own row
    52	* **(b)** An expression in `dab/uss.yaml`, emitted into the bridge by the generator
    53	* **(c)** Computed in the question's `uss.sql` at query time from two dates on the peripheral
    54	
    55	## Decision Outcome
    56	
    57	Chosen: **(a), a `NUMBER` attribute computed in the mapping** — with the precedent bounded here,
    58	because "M5 permits it" is otherwise the standing argument for whatever M5's regex happens not to
    59	catch.
    60	
    61	It is also the only option that generates today. A `sum` measure must name an attribute the model
    62	declares; `src/adss/uss.py` raises `KeyError: "ORDER has no attribute …"` otherwise, and there is
    63	no `expression:` field on a measure. (b) and (c) are not choices between working designs — they
    64	are proposals to build something.
    65	
    66	**Why not (b).** Putting the arithmetic in the generator is the serious rival, and it is cleaner in
    67	one respect: nothing derived is stored, so nothing derived can drift. It fails on where it leaves
    68	slice 6. A second source that reports elapsed days *directly* has no two dates for a DAR expression
    69	to subtract, so integrating it needs the attribute anyway — and then there are two definitions of
    70	ship lag, a DAB attribute and a DAR expression, differing by source. That is B2 and B8 failing
    71	together in the slice whose entire purpose is to prove B2. It also costs slice 4, where the
    72	expression vocabulary would have to grow from a two-date special case to general arithmetic in the
    73	same slice that first exercises the fan-out property D-0001 is carried on. Two risky things at once.
    74	
    75	A free-text SQL expression in YAML additionally breaks §3 — "SQL that lives in a Python string is
    76	written to a file so the same linter sees it" — because the linter runs on `.sql` files and would
    77	never see it.
    78	
    79	**Why not (c).** Conventions §2 says ratios are not stored and the numerator *is* an additive
    80	measure; (c) reads it as licence for the whole computation and has no `ship_lag_orders_days` at
    81	all. The question could then not declare what it measures: every `defines` entry must resolve to
    82	something the model or the sidecar defines, so "days to ship" would exist in one SQL file and
    83	nowhere else, with the page's own glossary unable to explain the second number it displays.
    84	
    85	The fatal objection is narrower. §6: "When a question's two queries disagree, `dab/model.yaml` is
    86	the arbiter. The query that departs from the definition is the one that changes." Under (c) the
    87	answer query says `date_diff('day', o.placed_on, o.shipped_on)`, the control says
    88	`shipped_date - order_date`, and the model has nothing to say about either. Neither query can
    89	depart from a definition that does not exist, so the repair procedure stops existing in exactly the
    90	slice that introduces the first computed number — and the cheapest repair becomes making the two
    91	queries agree with each other, which deletes the only thing the check measures.
    92	
    93	(c) also computes as of the wrong instant: the peripheral is current state, while a bridge row is
    94	the latest version *in which the event's date is set*. Those coincide today. ADR 0006 records a
    95	review catching precisely this confusion one layer down, and calls the distinction the entire
    96	difference between the option chosen there and the one rejected.
    97	
    98	### The line this record draws
    99	
   100	M5 permits an expression that reads its own row, and its prose enumerated three forms — a column,
   101	a cast, a `CASE` over columns of that row. A subtraction of two dates is none of them, and passes
   102	only because M5's mechanical check is four keywords and seven function names. Relying on that
   103	silently is the quiet exception §11 rules out. So the rule, in force from here:
   104	
   105	> **Arithmetic over columns of the same row is permitted in a mapping.** A `CASE`, a
   106	> default, a coalesce that invents a value, a filter, a bucket, or anything that changes the grain
   107	> is not — those are meaning, and meaning belongs in the model as an attribute with a definition.
   108	
   109	Conventions §1.4 M5 is clarified to say so, per §11's first rung. The distinction is that
   110	arithmetic over one row produces a value the row already implies; the others produce a value
   111	somebody chose, and a choice needs a definition beside it.
   112	
   113	`CASE` moves to the forbidden side, and the first draft of this record had it on both. M5
   114	permitted "a `CASE` over columns of that row" and the rule above forbade "a `CASE` on *values*" —
   115	but every `CASE` is over columns and on their values at once, so the pair decided nothing and
   116	handed back exactly the argument this section exists to close. By the test above a `CASE` is
   117	always a choice.
   118	
   119	One trap belongs in the record because the error message misleads: `extract(DAY FROM (b - a))` is
   120	**refused** by M5's checker, because the regex matches the bare word `from` inside the expression.
   121	The refusal says the expression "reaches beyond its row", which it does not. `date_diff('day', a,
   122	b)` passes and is what the mapping uses. The false refusal is a defect in the checker, fixed in
   123	this slice.
   124	
   125	## Consequences
   126	
   127	* Good, because the lag has one definition, in the one place the data is explained, and both of the
   128	  question's queries are measured against it
   129	* Good, because a second source that reports the lag directly maps onto the same attribute rather
   130	  than needing a second derivation — which is the slice-6 case that decided this
   131	* Good, because slice 4's revenue follows the same rule without a new mechanism: quantity, price
   132	  and discount are columns of one order line, and their product is arithmetic over that row
   133	* Good, because DAR stays deletable: everything it emits still comes from the model and the sidecar
   134	* Bad, because a derived value is now stored, and a stored derivation can disagree with what it was
   135	  derived from. Nothing today can make that happen — one mapping, one source — and it becomes
   136	  possible in slice 6
   137	* Bad, because the line above is a rule enforced by review. M5's checker cannot tell arithmetic
   138	  from a bucket, and writing a checker that could is a bigger thing than this slice needs
   139	
   140	## Confirmation
   141	
   142	`tests/test_mapping_rules.py` asserts that a same-row function is accepted and that the reaching
   143	forms are still refused, including the `extract(… FROM …)` case that used to be refused for the
   144	wrong reason.
   145	
   146	The two measures are `SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT` and `SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS`, and the ratio appears in no
   147	schema: the question returns both additive measures and the page divides them. That is not only
   148	§2's rule but what keeps the acceptance check exact — every value either query returns is a
   149	`BIGINT` count or an exact `DECIMAL` sum, and the two answers are compared row by row as values.
   150	A float would break that comparison in a way no test would find on the machine that wrote it:
   151	DuckDB's `sum` over doubles is order-dependent, measured here as `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` summing to
   152	`0.6000000000000001` and the same three reversed to `0.6`.
   153	
   154	Two things guard it, and it is worth being exact about which catches what. `tests/test_exactness.py`
   155	pins the predicate — a float is reported, a `Decimal` and a `bool` are not, every row is looked
   156	at, not only the first. That runs on every commit. The predicate is then applied to both answers
   157	of every question by a data check in `run_checks`, which runs after `adss build` rather than in
   158	the gate — so a float-valued measure fails `adss check`, not `pytest`, and it fails on the
   159	*values* returned rather than on a column's declared type.
   160	
   161	What is **not** confirmed, and is recorded rather than claimed: nothing checks that
   162	`SHIP_LAG_DAYS` still equals the two dates it was derived from. Such a check is tautological
   163	today — one mapping computes it from those columns and nothing else writes it — and stops being
   164	tautological in slice 6, which is the slice this decision's one real risk lands in. It is not
   165	written now because a check that cannot fail teaches a reader that the property is guarded when it
   166	is not; slice 6 writes it, against the case that makes it meaningful.

1	---
     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-08
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 3
     6	---
     7	
     8	# A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity, so two events on one entity may not name the same measure
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	Slice 3 is the first slice where one entity has two events: an order is both placed and shipped.
    13	That splits two things which have been the same thing until now.
    14	
    15	A measure's **column** and its **glossary token** are keyed on the entity:
    16	
    17	```python
    18	(event, measure, f"_measure__{event.entity_id.lower()}__{measure.id.lower()}")
    19	found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
    20	```
    21	
    22	Its **ownership** is keyed on the event — `_branch` decides which stage carries a value and which
    23	emits a typed null by identity on the event object. So the generator knows exactly which stage owns
    24	a measure, and then names it after something else.
    25	
    26	With one event per entity those keys coincide and nothing can go wrong. With two, declaring the
    27	same measure id on both events of one entity is accepted without a word, and produces:
    28	
    29	- **the same column twice** in the published contract, and
    30	- **one definition silently replacing the other** in the glossary.
    31	
    32	Reproduced on the neutral fixture. The column list came back with
    33	`_measure__parent__happened_parents_count` at two positions, and the glossary held the *second*
    34	event's definition under the first event's token.
    35	
    36	The two halves fail very differently. DuckDB does not refuse two columns of one name — measured,
    37	`CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS a` yields `a` and `a_1` — so the built table's columns would
    38	not match `bridge_columns()` and the contract check would fail the build loudly. That half is safe.
    39	
    40	**The glossary half is caught by nothing.** No check inspects `definitions()`. That dictionary is
    41	what a question's `defines` entries are resolved against, and what the page renders as "What the
    42	words mean". So a question could reference a measure, resolve it successfully, and be shown a
    43	definition belonging to a different measure — on the page a reader accepts the slice on — while
    44	every test and every check passes.
    45	
    46	Nothing enforces the naming convention that would prevent it either. Conventions §2's three-part
    47	pattern is a hard rule, and there is no test anywhere that checks a measure name's shape. The
    48	uniqueness of these columns has rested entirely on a rule enforced by reading.
    49	
    50	## Decision Drivers
    51	
    52	* a definition that is silently replaced is worse than one that is missing: nothing looks wrong
    53	* the failure must be loud where it is invisible, not only where DuckDB happens to complain
    54	* a published column contract two consumers are already written against
    55	* whatever is decided now is cheapest now, with two questions in existence
    56	
    57	## Considered Options
    58	
    59	* Refuse the collision when the declarations are read, and keep the entity in the column name
    60	* Rename the column to `_measure__<event>__<measure>` and the token to `<ENTITY>.<EVENT>.measures.<M>`
    61	* Do nothing, and rely on §2's naming pattern to keep ids distinct
    62	
    63	## Decision Outcome
    64	
    65	Chosen: **refuse the collision when the declarations are read.**
    66	
    67	Two events on one entity may not declare the same measure id. The refusal names both events and
    68	says what would be lost, because the loss is not obvious: a reader who has just been told the
    69	column would be duplicated will think of the column, and the definition is the part nothing else
    70	would catch.
    71	
    72	**Why not rename to the event.** It is more correct in principle — the event is what actually owns
    73	a measure, so the name should say so — and it is the cheapest it will ever be, with only two
    74	questions to update. It is rejected on two counts. It changes a published contract that conventions
    75	§1.3 states as a hard rule and ADR 0002 tabulates, in a slice that has no other reason to touch it.
    76	And §2's descriptor slot already carries the event: `placed_orders_count`, `shipped_orders_count`.
    77	Naming the column for the event too would put it in twice, so the more correct scheme reads worse
    78	in every ordinary case in order to disambiguate one that is now refused outright.
    79	
    80	**Why not do nothing.** §2's pattern makes a collision unlikely, not impossible, and "unlikely" is
    81	the wrong guarantee for a failure whose signature is a page showing a plausible sentence about the
    82	wrong number. Two events on one entity is exactly where the pattern's descriptor slot stops doing
    83	the work — `placed` and `shipped` distinguish the count measures, and nothing forces a third
    84	measure to carry a descriptor at all.
    85	
    86	This follows the shape the repository already uses for the same class of problem: ADR 0006 refuses
    87	two edges that would inherit into one key column, for the same reason and with the same argument
    88	about what DuckDB silently does instead of raising. A generator that cannot emit a correct artefact
    89	should say so rather than emit an ambiguous one.
    90	
    91	## Consequences
    92	
    93	* Good, because the glossary can no longer show one measure's definition under another's name,
    94	  which was the only failure here that nothing would have reported
    95	* Good, because it is a refusal in the same place and the same shape as the one for colliding
    96	  edges, so the two read as one rule rather than two special cases
    97	* Good, because it costs nothing today: no existing declaration collides, and no column moves
    98	* Bad, because it forbids a legitimate-sounding declaration — the same quantity measured at two
    99	  events, deliberately, under one name. That would have to be two measures with two definitions,
   100	  which is more honest but more typing. If a slice ever wants it, the answer is to rename to the
   101	  event, and this record is what it supersedes
   102	* Bad, because the deeper mismatch stays: the generator still names by entity what it owns by
   103	  event. This narrows the consequence to nothing rather than removing the cause
   104	
   105	### A correction to ADR 0002
   106	
   107	The same mismatch makes one sentence of ADR 0002's published column contract false, for the first
   108	time, in this slice. `_stage` is defined there as "the entity this row is a row *of*", and
   109	`_measure__<entity>__<measure>` is described as "non-null only on the owning stage". With two
   110	events on `ORDER` both branches emit `_stage = 'order'`, so all 809 shipped rows share a stage with
   111	the placed rows while carrying a null `_measure__order__placed_orders_count`. The column is
   112	non-null only on the owning **event**, which `_event` names and `_stage` does not. The contract's
   113	behaviour is right; that sentence describing it is not.
   114	
   115	## Confirmation
   116	
   117	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts that two events on one entity declaring one measure id are refused,
   118	and that the same id on two *different* entities is still accepted — which is the case the
   119	refusal must not catch, since `_measure__<entity>__` already distinguishes those.
   120	
   121	A second test asserts that `definitions()` returns one entry per declared measure, counting what
   122	the glossary returns rather than the declarations twice, so a silent overwrite fails on the count
   123	rather than on somebody reading a page carefully. That is the assertion that would have caught
   124	this, and it did not exist.
   125	
   126	Both of these were written wrong the first time and a review caught them, which is worth leaving in
   127	the record: the first named an acceptance case no fixture contained, and the second compared a list
   128	with itself. A Confirmation section that names a test is only as good as what the test actually
   129	constructs, and neither of these could have failed for the reason it was written down for.

1	---
     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-07
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 1
     6	---
     7	
     8	# daana-cli is the DAB engine, vendored as a checksum-pinned binary and constrained by a mapping rule set this repository enforces itself
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	DAB is where the three challenges are actually addressed, and Ensemble Modeling is how: a Core
    13	Business Concept holding only identity, a Description per attribute with its own history, an
    14	Association per relationship. The point of that decomposition is that change is additive — a new
    15	attribute is a new structure, never an `ALTER` to one other things depend on (blueprint B7).
    16	`daana-cli` implements exactly this shape, generating the structures and the loading code from a
    17	declared model, which is the "consistency by construction" the architecture depends on.
    18	
    19	Adopting it raises two problems that have nothing to do with modelling.
    20	
    21	The first is supply. The binary is a 174 MB git-LFS object on a private repository's branch. CI
    22	cannot reach it unauthenticated — raw, media and API all refuse — so the engine has to get into a
    23	build somehow, and the choice has consequences for anyone who ever clones this repository.
    24	
    25	The second is that the engine accepts several kinds of wrong mapping without complaint, and two of
    26	those are silent. `FULL` ingestion against a source view holding more than one row per key inserts
    27	one duplicate row per execute, forever, and **every presentation view hides it** — the current
    28	view and the history view both stayed the right size across three runs while the base table grew
    29	22 → 23 → 24 → 25. Our staged change log is multi-row-per-key by construction, so the wrong
    30	setting is the one that looks like a snapshot loader and is named after completeness. A mismatched
    31	relationship `source_table` is skipped in silence. Two `primary_keys` entries mean two alternate
    32	identifiers rather than a composite key, and that mode cannot be undone once loaded.
    33	
    34	Three further behaviours were observed on DuckDB, which the engine's own help text does not list
    35	among its supported platforms. `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` are created but never
    36	populated. `view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship keys despite its name. And if the
    37	process invoking the engine is itself holding the warehouse open, `execute` fails with
    38	`daana framework is not installed on the remote database`, which is not what went wrong.
    39	
    40	That last one was first reported to us in a broader form — that *any* other connection breaks it —
    41	and that turned out not to reproduce. DuckDB's lock is **per process**: within one process every
    42	connection shares an instance, so a second open succeeds; across processes the second is refused.
    43	The failure is therefore specific and enforceable: we must not hold the file while asking a
    44	subprocess to write to it. The narrower rule is the useful one, because it can be checked in code
    45	rather than believed.
    46	
    47	## Decision Drivers
    48	
    49	* a clone of this repository can build it, without a secret
    50	* the engine version is pinned by something that cannot be silently changed
    51	* the ways the engine accepts a wrong mapping are closed by this repository, not remembered
    52	* the DAB layer's history is what DAS observed, and is reproducible
    53	* a misleading engine error costs a reader minutes, not an afternoon
    54	
    55	## Considered Options
    56	
    57	* Vendor the binary here under git-LFS, restored in CI from a checksum-keyed cache
    58	* Fetch it in CI from the private source repository using a token secret
    59	* Two-tier CI: the gate always, the warehouse build only where the binary happens to exist
    60	* Require a local path and document it
    61	
    62	## Decision Outcome
    63	
    64	Chosen option: **vendor it here under git-LFS at `bin/linux-amd64/daana-cli`, with its `.sha256`
    65	beside it, restored in CI from an Actions cache keyed on that checksum.**
    66	
    67	The property that decides it is that the repository becomes self-contained: anyone who can clone
    68	it can build it, with no secret, no access to a second private repository, and no step that works
    69	only on the machine it was written on. For a system whose entire claim is reproducibility, an
    70	engine reachable only by the person holding a token is the wrong shape. Fetching with a secret was
    71	the serious alternative and it loses on exactly that — CI breaks for a fork, and for a future
    72	maintainer after a rotation, in a way that looks like a code failure. Two-tier CI loses harder:
    73	the check that actually proves the architecture works would be the one that does not run.
    74	
    75	The cost is real and is accepted: 174 MB of LFS storage, and a bandwidth bill on any run that
    76	misses the cache. Keying the cache on the checksum rather than on a version string means the
    77	transfer happens once per *binary*, and a changed binary invalidates the cache by construction
    78	rather than by anyone remembering to bump something.
    79	
    80	*The engine is pinned by content.* `daana-cli --version` self-reports `nightly` with a commit
    81	hash, so there is no version to depend on. `bin/linux-amd64/daana-cli.sha256` is the pin, it is
    82	verified before every invocation, and a mismatch is a hard failure rather than a warning. The
    83	self-reported string is recorded alongside it, so an upgrade is a diff that names both what
    84	changed and what it called itself.
    85	
    86	*The mapping rules are enforced here.* The seven rules in
    87	[conventions.md §1.4](../conventions.md) exist because the engine will not enforce them, and this
    88	repository checks them against `dab/mappings/*.yaml` in the machinery suite. `FULL_LOG` is the
    89	default and `FULL` requires a proof, because the failure it produces is invisible in every view a
    90	person would look at — including, and this is the part worth stating plainly, in both of a
    91	question's acceptance queries. The safety net would not have caught it.
    92	
    93	*DAR reads the `view_*` layer only.* Not `_focal`, not `_idfr`, not `_with_rel`. That is recorded
    94	here rather than in the DAR record because it is a fact about this engine on this platform, and it
    95	is where someone will look for it.
    96	
    97	*Entity ids stay `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`.* DuckDB preserves that casing into object names, so `view_ORDER`
    98	rather than `view_order`, where PostgreSQL would fold it. The convention survives because DuckDB
    99	resolves identifiers case-insensitively — a consumer may write either — but any code that matches
   100	names out of the catalog must normalise. Keeping the model's casing loud is worth more than the
   101	convenience: the visual break from every other layer's lower case is what makes a leak from DAB
   102	into DAS or DAR obvious on sight, which is the reason §1.2 asks for it.
   103	
   104	*Detached invocation.* The CLI refuses to invoke the engine while this process holds the
   105	warehouse, and says why. Destinations open read-only, which still holds the process lock but at
   106	least keeps a reader from writing. And the misleading error is translated: when the engine says
   107	the framework is not installed, we say the file is held, because that is what happened.
   108	
   109	### Consequences
   110	
   111	* Good, because anyone who can clone this repository can build it, with no secret and no second
   112	  repository
   113	* Good, because the engine is pinned by content, so it cannot change without the diff saying so
   114	* Good, because the seven mapping rules are checked by this repository's own tests rather than
   115	  remembered, which is what the architecture asks of every other convention
   116	* Good, because the engine's most misleading error now says what actually happened
   117	* Bad, because 174 MB of LFS storage is a real cost, and a cache miss is a real transfer. The
   118	  checksum key bounds it to once per binary, but it is not free
   119	* Bad, because a vendored binary is a supply-chain artefact in the repository. The `.sha256`
   120	  proves it has not changed; it does not prove it was ever trustworthy
   121	* Bad, because the build depends on three behaviours of an engine on a platform its own
   122	  documentation does not list. Each is pinned by a check, so a vendor change fails loudly — but it
   123	  will fail, and the fallback is a platform migration rather than a patch
   124	* Bad, because vendoring `linux-amd64` alone means this repository builds on one architecture.
   125	  Adding another is adding another 174 MB
   126	
   127	### Confirmation
   128	
   129	`tests/test_platform.py` reproduces the lock failure with DuckDB alone, no engine involved: a
   130	subprocess cannot write while this process holds the file, and can the moment it lets go.
   131	The binary is verified against the committed `.sha256` on every invocation, by `Engine.verify()`
   132	in `src/adss/engine.py`, and again in CI by `sha256sum -c` before anything runs it.
   133	`tests/test_engine_pin.py` does not hash the vendored binary itself — it is a 174 MB git-LFS
   134	object a fresh checkout need not have pulled, and section 6 says this suite touches no binary —
   135	so what it asserts is that a binary which does not match its record is refused, that one which
   136	does is accepted, and that the engine's self-report is written down beside it at all, since an
   137	engine with no version has nothing else to be identified by.
   138	
   139	`tests/test_mapping_rules.py` asserts six of the seven rules against every file in
   140	`dab/mappings/` — M6 concerns relationships and lands with the first one — including that
   141	`ingestion_strategy` is `FULL_LOG` and that `entity_effective_timestamp_expression` is
   142	`extracted_at`. A data check counts `dab.<ENTITY>_desc` against its own distinct
   143	(key, attribute, version) triples, because that base table is the only place the duplication
   144	defect is visible: every presentation view hides it, and so would both of a question's acceptance
   145	queries.
   146	# Architecture decision records
   147	
   148	One file per decision, numbered, in [MADR](https://adr.github.io/madr/) format. A record is
   149	**superseded by a new file, never edited**, because the value of a decision record is the record
   150	of what was true when it was made. A claim that turns out to be wrong is corrected in the record
   151	that found it wrong, named and quoted, rather than quietly rewritten where it stands — ADR 0006
   152	corrects two of ADR 0002's.
   153	
   154	**The Confirmation section is the one exception**, because it is not a record of anything: it is a
   155	claim about which checks exist *now*, and a stale one is a lie about the present rather than an
   156	honest account of the past. It is edited to match the checks, and only ever to match them. Twice
   157	already it had drifted the other way — describing a check somebody meant to write.
   158	
   159	An ADR lands **before** the code it decides. A decision record written afterwards records what
   160	was built, not what was decided.
   161	
   162	| # | Decision | Slice |
   163	|---|---|---|
   164	| [0000](0000-use-madr.md) | Decisions are recorded as MADR files in this directory | 0 |
   165	| [0001](0001-the-machinery-has-its-own-typed-domain.md) | The machinery is modelled in its own typed vocabulary, and no business word appears under `src/` | 1 |
   166	| [0002](0002-dar-is-one-generated-unified-star-schema.md) | DAR is one generated Unified Star Schema: an event bridge, peripherals, one calendar | 1 |
   167	| [0003](0003-a-das-contract-is-one-artefact.md) | A DAS contract is documentation, schema and transformation in one artefact | 1 |
   168	| [0004](0004-daana-cli-is-the-dab-engine.md) | daana-cli is the DAB engine, vendored and checksum-pinned | 1 |
   169	| [0005](0005-a-question-is-the-unit-of-delivery.md) | A business question is the unit of delivery, with two queries that must agree | 1 |
   170	| [0006](0006-an-inherited-key-is-resolved-as-of-the-row-that-inherits-it.md) | An inherited key is resolved from the raw pairs, as of the row that inherits it | 2 |
   171	| [0007](0007-a-derived-value-is-modelled-where-two-vocabularies-are-bound.md) | A value derived from one row is modelled in DAB and computed in the mapping | 3 |
   172	| [0008](0008-a-measure-is-owned-by-an-event-and-named-for-an-entity.md) | A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity, so two events on one entity may not share a measure id | 3 |

1	---
     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-07
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 1
     6	---
     7	
     8	# A DAS contract is documentation, schema and transformation in one artefact, and it generates a forgiving raw view plus a strict staged change log
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	Somewhere around the fifteenth staging table, hand-written SQL becomes a collection of
    13	undocumented micro-decisions nobody can reason about as a whole. A `COALESCE` wrapping a
    14	`SAFE_CAST` wrapping a JSON extraction might be handling a known source quirk or working around
    15	bad data that was hot-fixed months ago, and there is no way to tell, because the knowledge left
    16	with whoever wrote it. The contract exists to put that knowledge somewhere a person can read.
    17	
    18	Two blueprint principles pull in opposite directions here and the design has to satisfy both. S3
    19	says ingestion is forgiving and unpacking is strict: committing to a schema at ingest turns every
    20	upstream change into lost data, and enforcing nothing on the way out turns every upstream change
    21	into a silent one. S1 says DAS captures and persists *only* — no interpretation. A type cast sits
    22	uncomfortably between them, and the record has to say why it is capture rather than
    23	interpretation.
    24	
    25	The append-only rule (S2) creates the question this record most has to answer. After two loads the
    26	lake holds two copies of every unchanged record. Something downstream has to decide whether that
    27	is a change log or a duplicate, and the answer determines how DAB historizes — which makes it the
    28	most consequential thing in the layer.
    29	
    30	Two observations, both made against the real tools, close off the obvious implementations. `dlt`
    31	does not stop normalising when told to limit nesting: top-level keys are still split into inferred
    32	typed columns, and inference chose `DOUBLE` for a decimal money field. And `read_parquet` over a
    33	glob **silently drops** columns that appear only in later files — no error, no warning, just
    34	missing data — which is a correctness failure that an append-only lake will produce on its own the
    35	first time a column is added.
    36	
    37	## Decision Drivers
    38	
    39	* an upstream change must never lose data, and must never pass through unnoticed
    40	* the contract is the documentation, so there is nothing to keep in step with it
    41	* the layer must say what the source said, in the source's words
    42	* per-data-point provenance: from where, and when
    43	* every future engineer's staging decision is made once, in one place
    44	
    45	## Considered Options
    46	
    47	* One YAML contract generating a raw view over the payload plus a strict staged change log, with a `__current` projection beside it
    48	* `das__staged` deduplicated to one row per key, with the change log discarded
    49	* Letting the loader infer the schema and treating its output as the staged layer
    50	* Hand-written staging SQL per source table
    51	
    52	## Decision Outcome
    53	
    54	Chosen option: **one contract per source entity set, generating `das__raw.<table>`,
    55	`das__staged.<table>` as the change log, and `das__staged.<table>__current` beside it.**
    56	
    57	*`das__raw` is forgiving.* Each source record lands whole, as one JSON value in a `payload`
    58	column, alongside provenance the pipeline adds itself. Nothing is inferred, nothing is split, and
    59	a field the contract has never heard of still lands — it is simply not yet extracted. Schema drift
    60	becomes a contract edit rather than a pipeline failure, which is the whole point of S3's first
    61	half.
    62	
    63	*`das__staged` is strict.* One `cast(payload ->> '$.<SourcePath>' AS <TYPE>) AS <target_name>` per
    64	declared column, and nothing else. A column the contract does not declare does not exist
    65	downstream. `payload` is deliberately **absent** from the staged view: if it were present, a DAB
    66	mapping could read `payload ->> '$.X'` and bypass the contract entirely, and the contract would
    67	stop being the gate.
    68	
    69	This is where the S1 tension resolves. The cast is not interpretation, it is *transcription*: the
    70	contract records what the source's own metadata says a field is, and the cast makes the warehouse
    71	agree. The evidence that this is the right side of the line is that the alternative loses
    72	information — inference made a decimal into a floating-point number, silently, and money became
    73	approximate. Declaring `DECIMAL(18, 4)` in the contract recovers exactly what the source declared.
    74	What would cross the line is a `COALESCE`, a `CASE` on values, a filter or a default, and the
    75	contract format is structurally incapable of expressing any of them: there is no key for it.
    76	
    77	*The staged view is the change log, and `__current` sits beside it.* This is the consequential
    78	half. DAS is append-only, so the change log is what the layer actually holds, and it is what DAB
    79	historizes from — with `FULL_LOG`, which is idempotent against a multi-row-per-key source. The
    80	`__current` projection exists because a question asked *of the source* needs one row per thing,
    81	not one per observation; it is what the independent control query in every question file reads.
    82	Deduplicating `das__staged` itself was the alternative, and it fails on B3: the platform would
    83	then have no record of what it observed and when, and DAB's history would be reconstructed from
    84	something that had already thrown the observations away.
    85	
    86	### The provenance columns
    87	
    88	The pipeline adds these itself, and they are named for what they record rather than for whoever
    89	wrote them:
    90	
    91	| column | why |
    92	|---|---|
    93	| `source_system` | which system this came from. Answers half of "from where" without inference from a path |
    94	| `source_entity` | which entity set within it |
    95	| `source_url` | the request that produced the record |
    96	| `extracted_at` | when DAS observed it. Derived from the load id, and the clock DAB dates every version by |
    97	| `extracted_on` | the date of `extracted_at`, and the lake's hive partition key |
    98	
    99	`extracted_on` and `extracted_at` derive from the **same** fact, so they cannot disagree except
   100	across a midnight boundary — and the build asserts they do not. The loader's own bookkeeping
   101	columns stay in `das__raw` and do not cross into `das__staged`, because a loader's column name in
   102	the layer's published interface welds that loader into the layer everything else is rebuilt from.
   103	
   104	### Recording and replay
   105	
   106	A fixture is the recorded HTTP response body, page by page, exactly as the service returned it,
   107	under `das/fixtures/<table>/`, with a manifest keying each body to the request that produced it.
   108	**The recording is the default**: `adss das ingest` replays it, and `adss das ingest --live` reads
   109	the service. The two are otherwise the same code path — same resource, same contract, same
   110	landing, same request URLs — and that sameness is what makes the recording honest, because a
   111	replay that took a different path would prove nothing about the live run. A request the recording
   112	does not cover fails loudly rather than falling back to the network. `adss das record` refreshes a
   113	recording, and the diff on that commit is the source change, made visible.
   114	
   115	Defaulting to the recording rather than to the service is deliberate: the default is what runs in
   116	CI, on a plane, and on a day the demo service is down, and a build whose default reaches the
   117	network is a build a third party can fail.
   118	
   119	### Consequences
   120	
   121	* Good, because an upstream change lands rather than failing, and surfaces as an unextracted field
   122	  rather than as missing data
   123	* Good, because the contract is the documentation, the schema and the transformation, so there is
   124	  nothing that can drift from it
   125	* Good, because thirty tables share one set of staging decisions, and fixing a cast in the type
   126	  table fixes every contract that uses it
   127	* Good, because the change log preserves what the platform observed and when, which is what B3
   128	  needs and what a deduplicating staged view would have destroyed
   129	* Bad, because two staged objects per contract is more surface than one, and a reader has to know
   130	  which to use. The rule is short — DAB reads the change log, questions read `__current` — but it
   131	  is a rule
   132	* Bad, because `payload` being a plain string in the parquet means every strict read pays a JSON
   133	  parse. At this scale that is free; at a scale where it is not, this decision is what would need
   134	  revisiting
   135	* Bad, because the fixtures are a recording of a service that can change without telling us, so a
   136	  green offline build proves the code works, not that the source still looks like that. Only the
   137	  scheduled live run proves the second thing
   138	
   139	### Confirmation
   140	
   141	A machinery test generates the SQL for a neutral contract fixture and asserts the emitted
   142	expression for every type in the vocabulary, that `union_by_name => true` and `hive_types` are
   143	present, that the path is absolute, and that no key permitting an expression exists in the format.
   144	The contract reader itself refuses a dangling primary key, a `target_name` that is not the
   145	mechanical snake_case of its `source_path`, a type outside the closed vocabulary, and any key that
   146	could carry business logic.
   147	
   148	The contract also **generates its own data checks**, one per contract, into `checks/`: that
   149	`extracted_on` equals `cast(extracted_at AS DATE)` on every landed row, and that `__current` holds
   150	one row per key. They are generated rather than written because the machinery may not name a
   151	source, and emitted as files rather than strings because SQL in a string is SQL the linter never
   152	sees. `adss check` runs every one it finds, so a contract added in a later slice is checked
   153	without anything else changing.
